records.title: Contextualizing Period 1
records.text:
Contextualizing Period 1
What a historical context is, and the Native American, European, and African developments that framed the encounters of 1491 to 1607.
Encounters in the Americas began in a world already full of complex Native societies, competing European monarchies, and growing Atlantic trade. Placing an event in that setting is what contextualization means.
Every AP U.S. History period opens with a contextualizing topic. For Period 1 the question is what was already happening in the Americas, Europe, and Africa that shaped what happened when they met.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 1
records.heading: Context is the larger setting around a development
records.text:
Context is the larger setting around a development
A context is a described development that helps explain the topic, not a date or a vague phrase.
Contextualization means placing an event or process in the broader setting in which it happened. A strong context describes developments that came before, took place at the same time, or continued after the topic, and then connects them to it.
Take the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire (1519–1521). The completion of the Reconquista in 1492 is context from before: it joined Spanish military power to the goal of spreading Christianity. Spanish rivalry with Portugal for Atlantic wealth is context from the same period. The later flow of American silver to Europe shows how far the effects reached.
A date or a phrase is not a context. “Europeans wanted to explore” names no development. “After the Reconquista ended in 1492, the Spanish monarchy looked for wealth and converts beyond Iberia” describes one and ties it to the topic.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 1
records.heading: The Americas before 1491
records.text:
The Americas before 1491
Native societies were diverse and often complex before contact, and environment helped shape how each one lived.
Over thousands of years, Native peoples migrated across and settled North America. By 1491 they had built many distinct societies by adapting to, and reshaping, very different environments. Farmers in the Southwest irrigated maize fields. Peoples of the Northeast lived in permanent villages and combined farming with hunting. Peoples of the Northwest coast drew on the ocean's resources, and many Great Plains and Great Basin societies were largely mobile.
Some societies were large and complex. Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, was the center of a mound-building Mississippian society that traded across a wide region. In Mesoamerica and the Andes, the Aztec and Inca empires collected tribute from many peoples and governed large cities. Treating all of these peoples as one group hides the diversity that Europeans met.
Different environments led Native societies to develop different economies. Those economies in turn shaped where people lived, how they were governed, and how they would later respond to Europeans.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 1
records.heading: Europe, Africa, and the Atlantic
records.text:
Europe, Africa, and the Atlantic
Rivalry among European monarchies and growing Atlantic trade explain why Europeans crossed the ocean when they did.
In the late 1400s, European monarchies were competing for wealth, power, and religious leadership. Spain's rulers, Ferdinand and Isabella, united their kingdoms and completed the Reconquista in January 1492 by taking Granada. Portugal had already sent ships down the African coast, setting up trading posts for gold and, increasingly, enslaved people. Italian merchants and Muslim intermediaries controlled much of the trade with Asia, which gave Atlantic states a reason to seek other routes.
West African states such as Songhai and Kongo had their own trade networks, and slavery already existed in Africa, the Mediterranean, and Europe. Portuguese and Spanish colonists on Atlantic islands such as Madeira and São Tomé began growing sugar with enslaved African labor. This model later shaped labor in the Americas. The Protestant Reformation, which began in 1517, soon added religious conflict to the rivalry among European states.

records.title: Native American Societies Before European Contact
records.text:
Native American Societies Before European Contact
How maize, aridity, mixed farming, and ocean resources shaped the economies and settlements of Native American societies across North America before 1491.
Native societies did not share one way of life. Each adapted to its environment, and those adaptations produced very different economies, settlements, and social structures.
Learning objective B asks how and why native populations interacted with their natural environment. The strongest answers tie a region to its resources and then to the way people organized their lives.
records.excerpt: How maize, aridity, mixed farming, and ocean resources shaped the economies and settlements of Native American societies across North America before 1491.

records.title: Native American Societies Before European Contact
records.heading: Maize cultivation and the Southwest
records.text:
Maize cultivation and the Southwest
Maize and irrigation supported settlement and social diversification in the Southwest, without creating one political system.
Maize was first domesticated in what is now Mexico and spread north over centuries into the present-day American Southwest and beyond. Where farmers could water their fields, maize supported denser populations and permanent settlement.
The Hohokam of present-day Arizona dug long irrigation canals to bring river water to desert fields. Ancestral Puebloan peoples built multistory stone and adobe towns, such as the great houses of Chaco Canyon, and their descendants lived in pueblos such as Acoma. Surplus food allowed some people to work as builders, traders, and religious leaders, a change historians call social diversification.
Maize spread north, farmers developed irrigation, harvests grew, and settlements and specialized roles followed. These societies stayed politically separate and never formed a single Southwest empire.

records.title: Native American Societies Before European Contact
records.heading: Mobile societies of the Great Basin and Great Plains
records.text:
Mobile societies of the Great Basin and Great Plains
Aridity in the Great Basin and bison on the Plains led many societies to largely mobile lifestyles.
Much of the Great Basin is dry and offers little farmland. Shoshone, Paiute, and Ute families gathered seeds, pine nuts, and roots and hunted small game, moving in small groups with the seasons to follow scarce food.
On the grasslands of the western Great Plains, many peoples hunted bison, which required following the herds. Before horses arrived with Europeans, hunters traveled on foot and used fire and drives to take bison. Some Plains peoples, such as the Mandan, lived in river valleys and farmed as well as hunted, a reminder that one region could hold more than one way of life.

records.title: Native American Societies Before European Contact
records.heading: Mixed economies in the Northeast, Mississippi Valley, and Atlantic seaboard
records.text:
Mixed economies in the Northeast, Mississippi Valley, and Atlantic seaboard
A mix of farming, hunting, and gathering favored permanent villages in the East.
In the eastern woodlands and river valleys, many societies combined farming with hunting, fishing, and gathering. Maize, beans, and squash were grown together, and the food they supplied made permanent villages possible.
Mississippian peoples built large mounds and the city of Cahokia, which depended on maize and on trade across a wide region. In the Northeast, the Haudenosaunee lived in villages of longhouses. Algonquian-speaking peoples such as the Lenape and the Secotan of the Roanoke area moved seasonally to fish and hunt but kept fixed villages and fields.
Mixed economies were not the same as mobile ones. These societies farmed and kept permanent villages even when families traveled to hunt or fish.

records.title: Native American Societies Before European Contact
records.heading: The Northwest and California: ocean and river resources
records.text:
The Northwest and California: ocean and river resources
Abundant ocean and river resources supported settled communities without agriculture.
Along the Northwest coast, peoples such as the Chinook and the Tlingit relied on salmon, whales, shellfish, and forest products. These reliable resources let them live in settled communities with large plank houses and a rich trade in goods.
In California, many peoples, including the Chumash, supported dense populations without farming, relying on acorns, fish, and sea mammals. Neither region used maize, yet both developed settled and complex societies.

records.title: European Exploration in the Americas
records.text:
European Exploration in the Americas
Why Spain, Portugal, England, and France sent ships across the Atlantic: wealth, rivalry among monarchies, and the spread of Christianity.
European monarchies sought wealth, advantages over rivals, and religious expansion at the same time. Those motives overlapped, and together they explain why exploration became conquest.
The CED states one key concept for this topic: European efforts to explore and conquer the New World stemmed from a search for new sources of wealth, economic and military competition, and a desire to spread Christianity.
records.excerpt: Why Spain, Portugal, England, and France sent ships across the Atlantic: wealth, rivalry among monarchies, and the spread of Christianity.

records.title: European Exploration in the Americas
records.heading: Wealth, trade routes, and navigation
records.text:
Wealth, trade routes, and navigation
The search for wealth and trade routes, aided by new ships and navigation tools, sent Europeans across the Atlantic.
Spices, silk, and other Asian goods were valuable in Europe, and Italian merchants and Muslim intermediaries earned much of the profit. Rulers on the Atlantic edge of Europe wanted a share. Portugal sent ships down the African coast, and Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488. Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498.
Spain's rulers, Ferdinand and Isabella, agreed in 1492 to fund Christopher Columbus's plan to reach Asia by sailing west. Columbus reached islands in the Caribbean instead. New ships and tools made such voyages possible. The caravel's triangular sails let it sail against the wind, and the magnetic compass and astrolabe helped sailors find direction and latitude.
Competition for trade with Asia led monarchs to pay for new routes, better ships made long voyages possible, and the voyages brought Europeans into contact with the Americas.

records.title: European Exploration in the Americas
records.heading: Competition among European monarchies
records.text:
Competition among European monarchies
Rivalry pushed monarchies to claim territory quickly, and agreements between two states did not bind the others.
Strong monarchies saw overseas wealth as a way to pay armies and gain power over rivals. Portugal and Spain moved first. Pope Alexander VI's 1493 decree and the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 drew a line that gave Spain most lands to the west and Portugal lands to the east, which later gave Portugal claim to Brazil.
Other states ignored these agreements. England sponsored John Cabot's voyage to North America in 1497, and France sent Giovanni da Verrazzano in 1524 and Jacques Cartier in 1534. Each state claimed land by right of discovery, and each hoped to keep rivals from gaining the same wealth.
The treaty divided claims between two Catholic states. It did not stop France or England from sending their own expeditions.

records.title: European Exploration in the Americas
records.heading: Religion as a motive
records.text:
Religion as a motive
Religious goals strengthened the economic and political reasons for exploration and gave conquest a moral justification.
Many Europeans saw conquest and conversion as linked. Spain had just completed the Reconquista, the centuries-long Christian campaign against Muslim rule in Iberia, and its rulers carried that crusading spirit across the ocean. Catholic monarchs sent priests with soldiers, and they argued that they had a duty to convert the peoples they met.
After the Protestant Reformation began in 1517, religion also sharpened rivalry. Protestant England and Catholic Spain became opponents, and promoters of colonies, such as Richard Hakluyt in his 1584 Discourse Concerning Western Planting, argued that English settlements could spread Protestant Christianity and weaken Spain. Wealth, rivalry, and faith were rarely separate motives.

records.title: Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
records.text:
Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
What crossed the Atlantic after 1492, how epidemics and alliances made Spanish conquest possible, and how American silver and new business methods changed Europe's economy.
The Columbian Exchange moved crops, animals, and diseases between hemispheres. It strengthened European economies while devastating Native populations, and it made Spanish conquest possible.
This topic asks you to read claims about the Exchange and conquest. When you meet a source, ask what it claims, what evidence supports the claim, and what other factors it leaves out.

records.title: Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
records.heading: What crossed the Atlantic
records.text:
What crossed the Atlantic
The Exchange changed both hemispheres, but it did not affect them equally.
The Columbian Exchange was the movement of plants, animals, diseases, and people between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres that followed Columbus's voyages beginning in 1492. From the Americas came maize, potatoes, tomatoes, beans, cacao, and tobacco. From the Old World came wheat, sugar cane, horses, pigs, cattle, and sheep, along with diseases such as smallpox, measles, and influenza.
Potatoes and maize gave European farmers more food from the same land, which stimulated population growth. In the Americas, livestock changed how land was used, and wandering cattle and pigs sometimes damaged Native fields. Horses would later transform life for peoples of the Great Plains.
Voyages carried crops to Europe, and Europe's food supply and population grew. Voyages also carried diseases to the Americas, and Native populations fell sharply.

records.title: Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
records.heading: Epidemics and Spanish conquest
records.text:
Epidemics and Spanish conquest
Epidemics, Indigenous allies, and Spanish weapons together explain the fall of the Aztec and Inca empires.
Native peoples had no earlier exposure to Old World diseases, so epidemics spread quickly. In many regions most of the population died within a few generations. These losses weakened Native societies and made conquest easier.
In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with several hundred Spaniards, horses, and steel weapons. He won allies, such as the Tlaxcalans, who resented Aztec tribute demands. Smallpox struck Tenochtitlan in 1520, and the city fell in 1521. In the 1530s Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire, which had been weakened by disease and a civil war.
Spanish expeditions also reached what is now the United States. Ponce de León sailed to Florida in 1513, Hernando de Soto crossed the Southeast in 1539–1542, and Francisco Vázquez de Coronado explored the Southwest in 1540–1542. In 1565 Spain founded St. Augustine in Florida, the oldest continuously occupied European settlement in the continental United States.
Disease did not make conquest automatic. Spanish victories also depended on Indigenous allies, divisions among Native states, and Spanish weapons and horses.

records.title: Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
records.heading: Silver, trade, and a changing European economy
records.text:
Silver, trade, and a changing European economy
American silver and new business methods helped move Europe toward a market economy.
Spanish colonists found rich silver deposits at Potosí in the Andes, beginning in 1545, and at Zacatecas in Mexico. Silver flowed to Spain and then across Europe and to Asia, financing armies and expanding trade.
New methods of doing business spread too. Joint-stock companies let investors pool money for risky overseas ventures and share profits. Along with American crops and mineral wealth, these changes helped drive Europe's shift from feudalism, an economy built on land and obligations between lords and peasants, toward capitalism, an economy built on markets, money, and investment. The shift was gradual and uneven.

records.title: Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System
records.text:
Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System
How the encomienda, African slavery, and the casta system organized work and social rank across the Spanish empire in the Americas.
Spanish colonial economies were built on forced labor, first from Native Americans and then from enslaved Africans, and a rigid caste system ranked people by ancestry.
The CED asks how the growth of the Spanish empire shaped social and economic structures over time. Think about how labor, wealth, and rank connected.
records.excerpt: How the encomienda, African slavery, and the casta system organized work and social rank across the Spanish empire in the Americas.

records.title: Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System
records.heading: The encomienda and Native labor
records.text:
The encomienda and Native labor
The encomienda gave Spanish colonists control over Native labor and tribute, which fueled mining and plantation agriculture.
Spanish rulers rewarded conquistadors and settlers with grants called encomiendas. An encomienda gave a colonist the right to demand labor and tribute from a Native community. In return, the holder was supposed to protect the people and teach them Christianity, but in practice the system often meant brutal work and heavy losses of life.
Native workers mined silver, grew sugar and other crops, and herded livestock. In the Andes, Spanish officials adapted an Inca labor draft called the mita to supply workers for the silver mines at Potosí. Spain used Native labor to extract precious metals and to support plantation agriculture across its empire.
The encomienda was not slavery in law, because the Crown claimed Native peoples were its free subjects. In practice, forced and unpaid labor often looked much like slavery.

records.title: Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System
records.heading: Enslaved Africans in the Spanish and Portuguese Americas
records.text:
Enslaved Africans in the Spanish and Portuguese Americas
Labor shortages after Native population decline increased reliance on enslaved Africans obtained through partnerships on the African coast.
Slavery already existed in Africa, the Mediterranean, and Europe, and Portuguese traders had been buying enslaved Africans since the 1400s. Along the African coast, Europeans partnered with some West African groups that practiced slavery. These partners captured people and sold them to Europeans, who forcibly transported them across the Atlantic.
The Spanish began importing enslaved Africans to the Caribbean in the early 1500s. Demand grew as epidemics, overwork, and abuse reduced the Native workforce. Enslaved Africans labored on sugar plantations and in mines throughout the Spanish empire, and Portuguese colonists in Brazil built a large plantation economy on enslaved labor.
Native populations declined, labor shortages followed, and colonists and the Crown turned to enslaved Africans, which expanded the Atlantic slave trade.

records.title: Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System
records.heading: The casta system
records.text:
The casta system
The casta system defined each group's status by ancestry and tied social rank to rights, work, and taxes.
Spanish settlers formed families with Native and African partners, and the empire's population became very mixed. To organize this society, Spanish officials and the Church developed a caste system, known as the casta system, that ranked people by ancestry and color.
At the top were peninsulares, people born in Spain, who held the highest government and Church offices. Below them were criollos, people of Spanish descent born in the Americas. Mestizos had Spanish and Native ancestry, and mulattoes had Spanish and African ancestry. Native Americans paid tribute and provided labor, and enslaved Africans held the lowest position. Rank shaped legal rights, occupations, and taxes, though some people could improve their standing.

records.title: Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans
records.text:
Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans
How Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans misunderstood and borrowed from one another, how Native peoples defended their lands, and how Spanish leaders argued over the treatment of Native peoples.
Europeans and Native Americans held divergent worldviews, borrowed useful things from each other, and clashed over land and labor, while Europeans argued over how non-Europeans should be treated.
The CED asks you to explain how and why perspectives of others developed and changed. Look for what each side believed, what each side wanted, and how each side acted on those beliefs.

records.title: Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans
records.heading: Misunderstandings and borrowing
records.text:
Misunderstandings and borrowing
Different views of land, gender, religion, and trade produced misunderstandings, but each side also borrowed from the other.
In the early years of contact, each group tried to make sense of the other using its own assumptions. Europeans and Native Americans held divergent views about land use, gender roles, family, religion, and power, and these differences often produced misunderstandings.
Many Europeans believed land could be owned by individuals, fenced, bought, and sold. Many Native societies instead recognized shared rights to use land for farming, hunting, and gathering, and they did not see an agreement as giving up the land forever. Europeans also noticed that in many Native societies women farmed while men hunted and fought. Because European custom treated farming as men's work, many colonists judged Native societies as disordered or uncivilized. Native peoples often saw trade as a way to build lasting relationships through gifts and alliances, while Europeans emphasized profit.
Over time each side also adopted useful parts of the other's culture. Europeans learned to grow maize and other Native crops, and they borrowed Native knowledge of the land and its waters. Native peoples acquired European metal tools, cloth, and firearms, and, on the Plains, horses.
Misunderstanding did not mean that only Europeans failed to understand. Both sides misread the other, and each also borrowed what it found useful.

records.title: Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans
records.heading: Diplomacy and resistance
records.text:
Diplomacy and resistance
Native peoples defended their sovereignty through alliances and negotiation and through armed resistance.
As Europeans pressed onto Native lands and demanded Native labor, Native peoples worked to defend their political independence, their economies, their religious beliefs, and their ideas about gender relations. They used two main approaches: diplomatic negotiation and military resistance.
Diplomacy included trade agreements and alliances. Some Native leaders allied with Europeans to gain advantages over their own rivals. The Tlaxcalans, for example, joined Cortés against the Aztecs, whose tribute demands they resented. Military resistance took many forms. In 1598 Spanish settlers under Juan de Oñate entered the Pueblo lands of New Mexico and demanded food, goods, and labor. When warriors from Acoma Pueblo killed a group of Oñate's men, the Spanish attacked in January 1599, destroyed the pueblo, and enslaved many survivors.
European demands for land, labor, and religious change led Native peoples to negotiate when they could and to fight when they felt they must.

records.title: Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans
records.heading: The Spanish debate over treatment
records.text:
The Spanish debate over treatment
Spanish leaders disagreed about how to treat Native peoples, and the justifications for subjugating Africans and Native Americans came to include religious, cultural, and racial arguments.
Extended contact with Native Americans and Africans led Spanish religious and political leaders to argue over how non-Europeans should be treated. The Spanish Crown claimed the right to rule the Americas and to spread Christianity, and in 1513 royal lawyers drafted a document called the Requerimiento, which conquerors were told to read aloud to Native peoples. It demanded that they accept Spanish rule and the Christian faith or face war.
Some Spaniards condemned the cruelty of the colonial system. The Dominican friar Bartolomé de las Casas, who had seen the abuse of Native workers, argued that Native peoples were rational human beings who should be converted by persuasion, not by force. His writings influenced the New Laws of 1542, which restricted new encomiendas and tried to limit abuse, though colonists resisted and enforcement was weak. Las Casas at first suggested that enslaved Africans could ease the burden on Native workers, a view he later condemned. Others, such as the scholar Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, argued that Native peoples were naturally inferior and could justly be ruled and made to work. The two men presented their arguments in a famous debate at Valladolid in 1550–1551.
Over time, the justifications used to subjugate Native Americans and Africans changed and combined religious, cultural, and racial arguments. Defenders of conquest and slavery claimed they were civilizing and converting people they described as inferior, and these ideas about race became more important as slavery expanded.

records.title: Causation in Period 1
records.text:
Causation in Period 1
How to explain the causes and effects of the transatlantic voyages of 1491–1607: separating long-term and short-term causes, tracing chains of effects, and weighing competing explanations.
Historians explain events by identifying several causes, separating what made an event possible from what made it happen, and judging which causes mattered most.
This topic applies the reasoning skill of causation to everything in Unit 1. The CED asks you to explain the effects of the development of transatlantic voyages from 1491 to 1607.

records.title: Causation in Period 1
records.heading: Why the voyages began
records.text:
Why the voyages began
Exploration had several long-term causes, and a short-term decision set particular voyages in motion.
Causation means explaining why something happened and what it led to. Most events have more than one cause, and causes differ in how long they were at work. Long-term causes built over many years. Short-term causes were closer to the event and often triggered it.
The long-term causes of European exploration were the search for new sources of wealth, economic and military competition among monarchies, and a desire to spread Christianity. A short-term trigger was a particular decision, such as Ferdinand and Isabella's agreement in 1492 to fund Columbus. Better ships and navigation tools, such as the caravel and the compass, were conditions that made long voyages possible, but they do not explain why rulers wanted to pay for them.
Do not confuse what made an event possible with what made it happen. Technology made the voyages possible. Wealth, rivalry, and faith gave monarchs reasons to send them.

records.heading: From voyages to an Atlantic world
records.text:
From voyages to an Atlantic world
Effects of the voyages linked together in chains, and some of the most important ones were unintended.
The voyages produced effects that unfolded in stages. Contact quickly brought the Columbian Exchange. Old World diseases spread through Native populations that had no immunity, and in many regions most of the people died within a few generations. These losses, together with Indigenous alliances and Spanish weapons, made conquest possible.
Conquest led to further effects. Spain built an empire that depended on forced labor. Labor shortages after Native population decline increased the demand for enslaved Africans, which expanded the Atlantic slave trade and strengthened the role of some West African partners in supplying captives. American silver and crops helped change Europe's economy, and new business methods such as joint-stock companies spread. Over time, the voyages linked Europe, Africa, and the Americas in one Atlantic world.
Voyages carried diseases to the Americas, Native populations fell, labor shortages followed, and Spain imported more enslaved Africans. Each effect became a cause of the next development.
Rulers intended to gain wealth and spread Christianity. They did not intend the epidemics that spread among Native peoples, although the epidemics helped the conquest succeed.

records.title: Causation in Period 1
records.heading: Weighing causes and making a causal claim
records.text:
Weighing causes and making a causal claim
To make a causal claim, name the cause and effect, explain the link, and weigh it against other causes with evidence.
When several causes explain an event, historians judge which mattered most. Consider the fall of the Aztec Empire. Some historians stress disease, because epidemics killed many Aztecs and weakened the city. Others stress Indigenous allies, such as the Tlaxcalans, because thousands of Native warriors fought alongside a small Spanish force. Most agree that weapons, allies, and disease worked together, but they disagree about how much weight each deserves.
A strong causal claim names a cause and an effect, explains the link between them, and supports the link with specific evidence. For example, a claim that competition among monarchies drove exploration should point to specific actions, such as Spain and Portugal dividing the world in the Treaty of Tordesillas and England and France sending their own expeditions despite it.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 2
records.text:
Contextualizing Period 2
The context for European colonization of North America from 1607 to 1754: what had already happened, what each empire wanted, and how environment and rivalry shaped the colonies.
Different European empires brought different goals for land and labor to North America, and competition over resources shaped relations with American Indians and with one another.
A context describes the broader developments before, during, and after the period that help explain an event. Period 2 covers 1607 to 1754, when European colonies took root and grew.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 2
records.heading: What had already happened by 1607
records.text:
What had already happened by 1607
Spanish wealth, English rivalry with Spain, religious conflict, and economic pressure helped set the stage for colonies in North America.
By 1607, Spain had ruled much of Mexico, the Caribbean, and South America for nearly a century and was bringing silver across the Atlantic. Spanish settlers had founded St. Augustine in Florida in 1565. English leaders, who envied Spain's wealth, had tried and failed to plant a colony at Roanoke in the 1580s, and in 1588 England's navy helped defeat the Spanish Armada, a fleet Spain had sent against England.
Religious conflict also pushed migration. The Protestant Reformation had divided Europe, and in England Puritans wanted to reform the Church of England while Separatists wanted to leave it. In addition, English economic troubles, including a growing population and unemployment, led some people to look for opportunity overseas.
Contextualization is not a list of earlier events. It explains how those developments help account for the thing you are studying.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 2
records.heading: Different empires, different goals
records.text:
Different empires, different goals
Spain sought wealth and subjects, France and the Netherlands sought trade, and Britain sought settlement and agriculture.
Spain's goal was to extract wealth from the land. Its institutions subjugated Native populations, converted them to Christianity, and incorporated them, along with enslaved and free Africans, into Spanish colonial society.
France and the Netherlands pursued trade. Few French and Dutch colonists crossed the ocean, and they built economic and diplomatic ties with American Indians to obtain furs and other goods for export to Europe. Britain sent far larger numbers of migrants, men and women, who wanted land, prosperity, religious freedom, and a better life. English colonists focused on agriculture and settled on land taken from Native Americans.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 2
records.heading: Environment, resources, and rivalry
records.text:
Environment, resources, and rivalry
Varied environments and competition for resources shaped colonial economies and set the stage for trade and conflict.
North America offered varied environments, from cold northern forests to warm southern coasts and fertile river valleys. Each region supported different products, such as furs, grain, fish, tobacco, and rice, and those products shaped how colonies earned money and what kind of labor they used.
Europeans competed with one another and with American Indians for resources such as land, furs, and fishing grounds. That competition encouraged industry and trade, but it also led to conflict. American Indian nations joined Europeans as allies, traded with them, and sometimes fought them to protect their own interests.

records.text:
European Colonization
How Spanish, French, Dutch, and English colonization differed in size, goals, labor, and relations with American Indians.
Spain built institutions of conquest and conversion, France and the Netherlands built small trading colonies, and England built agricultural colonies filled with migrants who took Native land.
The CED asks you to explain how and why various European colonies developed and expanded. Compare what each empire wanted, who came, and how they treated Native peoples.

records.title: European Colonization
records.heading: Spanish colonies in the borderlands
records.text:
Spanish colonies in the borderlands
Spain used conquest, conversion, and forced labor to subordinate Native peoples inside a ranked colonial society.
Spain's colonial system rested on extracting wealth from the land. In what is now the United States, Spain founded St. Augustine in Florida in 1565, and in 1598 Juan de Oñate led settlers into New Mexico, where Santa Fe became the capital in 1610. Spanish officials built institutions that subjugated Native peoples, converted them to Christianity through missions, and incorporated them, along with enslaved and free Africans, into colonial society.
The Spanish ranked people by ancestry and demanded Native labor and tribute. Franciscan missionaries tried to replace Native religious practices. Spanish settlements in the borderlands were small and often served as military outposts to protect Spain's richer colonies farther south.

records.title: European Colonization
records.heading: French and Dutch trading colonies
records.text:
French and Dutch trading colonies
France and the Netherlands built small colonies that depended on trade alliances and family ties with Native peoples.
France founded Quebec in 1608, and the Dutch founded New Netherland, with its port of New Amsterdam, in the 1620s under the Dutch West India Company. Both colonies attracted relatively few Europeans. Their goal was the fur trade, not large farming settlements, so colonists relied on trade alliances and on marriage and family ties with American Indians to acquire furs and other products for export to Europe.
French traders and Jesuit missionaries traveled deep into the interior and allied with nations such as the Huron and Algonquin. The Dutch traded with the Iroquois at Fort Orange, near present-day Albany. Because these colonies needed Native partners, their relations with American Indians were more cooperative than in English colonies, although alliances also drew Native peoples into European rivalries.
French and Dutch cooperation with American Indians was practical, not equal. Colonists wanted furs, and trade changed Native economies and sometimes led to conflict.

records.title: European Colonization
records.heading: English settlement colonies
records.text:
English settlement colonies
England sent many families who farmed land taken from American Indians, which led to conflict over land.
England founded Jamestown in Virginia in 1607, Plymouth in 1620, and Massachusetts Bay in 1630. Unlike the Spanish, French, and Dutch, England attracted a comparatively large number of migrants, including many women and families, as well as other Europeans. They came seeking social mobility, economic prosperity, religious freedom, and better living conditions.
Private joint-stock companies, such as the Virginia Company, paid for early ventures. English colonists focused on agriculture, settled on land taken from Native Americans, and lived separately from them. This pattern of settlement caused more direct conflict over land than the trade-based French and Dutch colonies did.

records.title: The Regions of British Colonies
records.text:
The Regions of British Colonies
How environment, religion, labor, and distance from Britain produced the Chesapeake, New England, middle, and southern plantation colonies and their self-governing institutions.
The British colonies developed distinct regions because of different environments, motives, and labor systems, and distance from Britain let all of them build self-governing institutions.
The CED asks you to explain how and why environmental and other factors shaped the development of the British colonies. For each region, ask what the land produced, who did the work, and how the colony governed itself.

records.title: The Regions of British Colonies
records.heading: The Chesapeake and North Carolina: tobacco
records.text:
The Chesapeake and North Carolina: tobacco
Tobacco drove the Chesapeake economy, first with indentured servants and later with enslaved Africans.
Virginia and Maryland, the Chesapeake colonies, and North Carolina grew prosperous by exporting tobacco. Jamestown struggled until John Rolfe's tobacco found a market in England, after which planters rushed to claim land. Tobacco was labor-intensive, and at first it was grown mainly by white, mostly male indentured servants who signed contracts to work for a set number of years in exchange for passage.
Later, as fewer servants came and planters wanted a permanent workforce, enslaved Africans increasingly replaced indentured servants. Because most of the early migrants were men, the Chesapeake had unequal numbers of men and women and high death rates from disease.
Indentured servitude was not slavery. Servants worked under contract for a limited time, while slavery was permanent and hereditary.

records.title: The Regions of British Colonies
records.heading: New England: towns and a mixed economy
records.text:
New England: towns and a mixed economy
New England's Puritan towns and family farms supported a mixed economy of agriculture and commerce.
Puritans settled New England beginning in the 1620s and 1630s, seeking to build religious communities. Colonists settled in small towns and farmed family-sized plots on rocky soil with short growing seasons. They did not grow a single export crop. Instead they built a thriving mixed economy of agriculture, fishing, shipbuilding, lumber, and trade.
Many families migrated together, and the New England population was healthier and more balanced than the Chesapeake's. Town meetings, where male landholders discussed local affairs, shaped local government.

records.title: The Regions of British Colonies
records.heading: The middle colonies: grain and diversity
records.text:
The middle colonies: grain and diversity
Grain exports and migration from many places made the middle colonies diverse and relatively tolerant.
New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Delaware had fertile soil and a longer growing season than New England. Their farmers raised cereal crops, especially wheat, and exported grain and flour, which gave the middle colonies a flourishing export economy. William Penn founded Pennsylvania in 1681 as a refuge for Quakers.
Because their land and trade drew migrants from many places, the middle colonies became more diverse than New England or the South. English, Dutch, German, Scots-Irish, and other settlers, with Protestants of many denominations and some Jews and Catholics, lived side by side, which led to greater cultural, ethnic, and religious diversity and tolerance.

records.heading: The southern Atlantic coast and the West Indies: plantations
records.text:
The southern Atlantic coast and the West Indies: plantations
Long growing seasons produced cash-crop plantations that relied on enslaved Africans, who were often the majority.
South Carolina, Georgia, and the British West Indies had long growing seasons that supported plantation economies based on exporting cash crops. South Carolina planters grew rice and, later, indigo. In the West Indies, planters on islands such as Barbados and Jamaica grew sugar.
These plantations depended on the labor of enslaved Africans, who often made up the majority of the population in these areas. Enslaved people developed their own forms of cultural and religious autonomy, blending African traditions with new surroundings.

Self-government at a distance
Weak British oversight let colonists build assemblies and town meetings that were unusually democratic for the era.
Distance and Britain's initially lax attention let the colonies create self-governing institutions that were unusually democratic for the era. In Virginia, the House of Burgesses first met in 1619. In New England, power rested in participatory town meetings, whose members elected representatives to colonial legislatures. In the southern colonies, elite planters exercised local authority and also dominated the elected assemblies.
Voting was limited, usually to white men who owned property, but a much larger share of colonists could vote than in Britain. Colonial assemblies gained experience in taxing and spending, which later shaped how colonists reacted to British control.

records.title: Transatlantic Trade
records.text:
Transatlantic Trade
How an Atlantic economy linked Europe, Africa, and the Americas, how Britain tried to control it through mercantilism, and how trade changed American Indian communities.
Atlantic trade tied the colonies to Europe and Africa, Britain tried to run that trade for its own benefit through mercantilism, and trade transformed Native communities.
The CED asks you to explain causes and effects of transatlantic trade over time. Follow the goods and the people: who produced them, who bought them, and who profited.

records.title: Transatlantic Trade
records.heading: An Atlantic economy
records.text:
An Atlantic economy
Colonial commodities, manufactured goods, and enslaved people moved through a web of Atlantic trade.
An Atlantic economy developed in which goods, along with enslaved Africans and American Indians, moved among Europe, Africa, and the Americas through extensive trade networks. European colonial economies focused on acquiring, producing, and exporting commodities that were valued in Europe, such as tobacco, sugar, rice, furs, fish, and timber, and on gaining new sources of labor.
Ships carried manufactured goods from Europe to Africa and the Americas, enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to the colonies, and colonial products back to Europe. Many voyages did not follow a neat triangle, and merchants also traded directly between colonies and the West Indies, but historians use the term triangular trade for this web of exchange. Some colonists also captured and sold American Indians as slaves, as in the Carolina trade, which sent many to the Caribbean.
The triangular trade is a model of connected routes, not a single fixed route that every ship followed.

records.title: Transatlantic Trade
records.heading: Mercantilism and imperial control
records.text:
Mercantilism and imperial control
Britain used the Navigation Acts to make the colonies serve its economy, but weak and uneven enforcement left colonists room to resist.
Britain, like other European powers, followed mercantilism, the belief that a nation grows strong by exporting more than it imports and by using colonies to supply raw materials and buy its manufactured goods. To pursue those aims, Parliament passed the Navigation Acts beginning in 1651 and 1660. They required that colonial trade travel on English or colonial ships and that certain valuable goods, such as tobacco and sugar, be shipped only to England or other English colonies.
Britain tried to fit its North American colonies into a coherent, hierarchical imperial structure, but enforcement was erratic. Conflicts with colonists and American Indians, the long distance across the Atlantic, and Britain's own distractions meant that smuggling was common and many rules went unenforced. Britain's occasional efforts to tighten control, such as the Dominion of New England in the 1680s, met resistance.

records.title: Transatlantic Trade
records.heading: Trade and American Indian communities
records.text:
Trade and American Indian communities
Trade changed Native economies and cultures, and it spread epidemic disease that reshaped Native populations.
Continuing trade with Europeans increased the flow of goods in and out of American Indian communities. Native peoples traded furs and deerskins for metal tools, cloth, and guns. This trade stimulated cultural and economic change, such as dependence on European goods and shifts in hunting patterns.
Contact also spread epidemic diseases that caused radical demographic shifts, killing large shares of some communities. Competition for trade goods and hunting grounds also sharpened rivalries among Native nations and among European empires.

records.title: Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans
records.text:
Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans
How alliances, trade, and war shaped relations among American Indian nations and French, Dutch, British, and Spanish colonies, including Metacom's War and the Pueblo Revolt.
American Indian nations acted for their own interests, forming alliances and fighting wars with European colonies, and their resistance shaped how colonial societies developed.
The CED asks you to explain how and why interactions between European nations and American Indians changed over time. When you read a source about these events, ask who wrote it, for whom, and why, because each side saw events differently.

records.title: Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans
records.heading: Alliances and accommodation
records.text:
Alliances and accommodation
Europeans and American Indians formed alliances for their own purposes, and those alliances brought both cooperation and conflict.
Interactions between European rivals and American Indian nations fostered both accommodation and conflict. French, Dutch, British, and Spanish colonies allied with and armed American Indian groups, and Native nations frequently sought alliances with Europeans against other American Indian nations.
The French and their Algonquin and Huron allies fought the Iroquois Confederacy, also called the Haudenosaunee, which traded with the Dutch at Fort Orange and later with the English. In the late 1600s the Iroquois and English colonists joined in a diplomatic alliance known as the Covenant Chain. In Virginia, the Powhatan Confederacy traded with Jamestown's settlers, but conflicts over land and food led to wars, including a Powhatan attack in 1622 that killed hundreds of colonists.
American Indians were not passive partners. Nations chose alliances to protect their land and trade, and they often bargained with several European powers at once.

records.title: Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans
records.heading: Metacom's War
records.text:
Metacom's War
Conflict over land and authority led to Metacom's War, which devastated both sides and ended Native power in southern New England.
By the 1670s English settlements in New England had grown, and colonists were pressing onto Native land, extending English law over Native peoples, and pushing Native communities to adopt Christianity. Metacom, a Wampanoag leader whom the English called King Philip, resisted these pressures. In 1675 fighting began after the English executed three Wampanoag men, and it spread across New England as the Wampanoag, Narragansett, Nipmuc, and other nations attacked English towns.
Colonists, aided by Native allies such as the Mohegan, struck back, and the war ended in 1676 when Metacom was killed. Thousands of people died, including a large share of the colonial and Native populations, and English towns were destroyed. British conflicts with American Indians over land, resources, and political boundaries had led to a military confrontation, and its outcome broke the power of Native nations in southern New England, where many captives were enslaved or sold.

records.title: Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans
records.heading: The Pueblo Revolt and Spanish accommodation
records.text:
The Pueblo Revolt and Spanish accommodation
The Pueblo Revolt expelled the Spanish for a time and led Spain to accommodate some Pueblo culture after its return.
In New Mexico, Spanish colonists demanded labor and tribute from Pueblo peoples, and Franciscan priests tried to suppress Native religious ceremonies. In 1680, Pueblo communities, led in part by a religious leader named Popé, rose together, killed hundreds of Spanish colonists, including many priests, and drove the Spanish out of New Mexico.
The Spanish returned in 1692 and 1693, but Pueblo resistance changed their approach. Spanish officials reduced forced labor demands and tolerated some Pueblo religious practices alongside Catholicism. American Indian resistance, particularly after the Pueblo Revolt, led to Spanish accommodation of some aspects of American Indian culture in the Southwest.

records.title: Slavery in the British Colonies
records.text:
Slavery in the British Colonies
How slavery spread through the British colonies, how colonial laws created a racial system of chattel slavery, and how enslaved Africans resisted and preserved their culture.
Slavery grew because land was abundant and labor was scarce, colonial laws made it hereditary and racial, and enslaved people resisted it openly and in everyday ways while preserving their own culture.
The CED asks you to explain the causes and effects of slavery in the British colonial regions and how enslaved people responded. Keep each region's economy in mind.

records.title: Slavery in the British Colonies
records.heading: The slave trade and the colonies
records.text:
The slave trade and the colonies
Land, demand for colonial goods, and a shortage of servants drew all British colonies into the slave trade, with plantation regions using the most enslaved labor.
All the British colonies took part to varying degrees in the Atlantic slave trade. The reasons were an abundance of land, a growing European demand for colonial goods, and a shortage of indentured servants. Enslaved Africans endured the Middle Passage, the forced voyage across the Atlantic, in crowded and unhealthy ships, and many died on the way.
The extent of slavery depended on the economy. Small New England farms used relatively few enslaved laborers, and all port cities held significant minorities of enslaved people. The emerging plantation systems of the Chesapeake and the southern Atlantic coast had large numbers of enslaved workers. The great majority of enslaved Africans, however, were sent to the West Indies.

records.title: Slavery in the British Colonies
records.heading: Chattel slavery and the law
records.text:
Chattel slavery and the law
Colonial laws made slavery a racial, hereditary, lifelong status.
In the early 1600s the legal status of Africans in Virginia was unsettled, and some became free. As chattel slavery, in which people are legal property and slavery is lifelong, became the dominant labor system in many southern colonies, new laws created a strict racial system. Slave codes restricted where enslaved people could go and what they could do, and they prohibited interracial relationships. A Virginia law of 1662 defined the children of enslaved mothers as enslaved, so slavery passed from mother to child. In this way the descendants of African American mothers were defined as black and enslaved in perpetuity.
Many historians argue that planters' fear of unrest also pushed them toward slavery. In Bacon's Rebellion in 1676, poor white and Black laborers in Virginia joined an armed revolt against the colonial elite, and afterward planters relied more heavily on African slavery, which also let them use race to divide laborers.
Slavery was not simply a leftover of earlier labor systems. Colonial legislatures wrote laws that made it racial, hereditary, and permanent.

records.title: Slavery in the British Colonies
records.heading: Resistance and culture
records.text:
Resistance and culture
Enslaved people resisted through revolt, flight, and daily acts of defiance and kept their families, cultures, and religions alive.
Africans developed both overt and covert means to resist the dehumanizing nature of slavery. Overt resistance included armed revolt. In 1739, in the Stono Rebellion in South Carolina, a group of enslaved people seized weapons, killed several colonists, and marched toward Spanish Florida before militia defeated them. South Carolina responded with a harsher slave code. Others fled to Spanish Florida, where Spain offered freedom to those who converted to Catholicism.
Covert resistance included working slowly, damaging tools, feigning illness, and learning in secret. Enslaved people also maintained their family and gender systems, culture, and religion. African languages, music, foods, and names blended with new influences, as in the Gullah culture of the South Carolina coast, and enslaved people formed their own religious communities.

records.title: Colonial Society and Culture
records.text:
Colonial Society and Culture
How religious and ethnic diversity, the Great Awakening, Enlightenment ideas, print, and Anglicization shaped colonial culture and prepared colonists to question British control.
Diversity, religious revival, Enlightenment ideas, and English political habits bound the colonies to Britain and to each other, even as they gave colonists reasons to resist imperial control.
The CED asks you to explain how the movement of people and ideas across the Atlantic shaped American culture and how colonists viewed their relationship with Britain. Notice what pulled the colonies closer to Britain and what pushed them away.

records.title: Colonial Society and Culture
records.heading: Pluralism and the Great Awakening
records.text:
Pluralism and the Great Awakening
Religious and ethnic pluralism, deepened by the Great Awakening, gave colonists more religious independence and common experience.
The presence of different European religious and ethnic groups, including English Anglicans and Puritans, Dutch Reformed, German Lutherans, Scots-Irish Presbyterians, Quakers, and Catholics, contributed to a significant degree of pluralism and intellectual exchange in the colonies. No single church could claim the loyalty of everyone.
In the 1730s and 1740s the First Great Awakening, a wave of Protestant revivals, swept the colonies. Preachers such as Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield urged listeners to seek a personal religious experience. Edwards's 1741 sermon "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" warned that sinners depended on God's mercy. The Awakening divided congregations between supporters and critics, challenged established ministers, increased religious independence and diversity, and gave colonists a shared experience across colonial boundaries.
The Great Awakening was a religious movement, not a political one, but it taught colonists to question established authority and to organize on their own.

records.title: Colonial Society and Culture
records.heading: Enlightenment ideas and print culture
records.text:
Enlightenment ideas and print culture
Enlightenment ideas and a growing print culture connected colonists to Europe and to each other.
The European Enlightenment, an intellectual movement that stressed reason, observation, and natural rights, also spread to the colonies. Benjamin Franklin conducted scientific experiments and helped found the American Philosophical Society in 1743. Colonial readers studied the writings of English thinkers, including John Locke, who argued that government rested on the consent of the governed and existed to protect natural rights.
A transatlantic print culture linked the colonies to Britain and to one another. Colonial newspapers, almanacs, and pamphlets spread news and ideas, and in 1735 a New York jury acquitted the printer John Peter Zenger of libel after he criticized the royal governor, which strengthened ideas about a free press.

records.title: Colonial Society and Culture
records.heading: Anglicization and growing mistrust
records.text:
Anglicization and growing mistrust
Colonists became more English in their institutions, yet their experiences and ideas also gave them grounds to resist imperial control.
Over time the British colonies experienced a gradual Anglicization, developing autonomous political communities based on English models, with elected assemblies, English law, and English customs. Intercolonial commercial ties, the print culture, and the spread of Protestant evangelicalism also helped bind the colonies to Britain and one another.
At the same time, the goals and interests of European leaders and colonists diverged, leading to a growing mistrust on both sides of the Atlantic. Colonists, especially in British North America, were dissatisfied over issues such as territorial settlements, frontier defense, self-rule, and trade. Their resistance drew on local experience of self-government, evolving ideas of liberty, the political thought of the Enlightenment, greater religious independence and diversity, and a belief that the imperial system was corrupt.

records.title: Comparison in Period 2
records.heading: How to compare
records.text:
How to compare
A comparison needs a criterion, similarities, differences, and reasons that explain them.
Comparison means explaining similarities and differences between developments. A strong comparison starts with a criterion, such as labor, religion, or relations with American Indians, so that the things you compare are measured against the same standard. Then it names at least one similarity and one difference and explains why they existed. Listing facts about each subject separately is description, not comparison.
Do not stop after naming a difference. Explain why it existed, for example because of environment, goals, or labor needs, and say why it mattered.

records.title: Comparison in Period 2
records.heading: Comparing European colonization
records.text:
Comparing European colonization
All empires sought wealth, but the form of their colonies, and their relations with Native peoples, differed with their goals.
Spain, France, the Netherlands, and Britain all wanted wealth, and all used American Indians as trading partners, workers, or allies. They differed in how they pursued their goals. Spain extracted wealth through conquest, missions, and forced labor and incorporated Natives and Africans into a ranked society. France and the Netherlands sent few colonists and relied on trade alliances and family ties to obtain furs. Britain sent many families who took land for farming, lived apart from Native peoples, and fought over land.
These differences help explain why relations with American Indians varied. Colonies built around trade needed Native partners, while colonies built around land and farming needed Native land.

records.title: Comparison in Period 2
records.heading: Comparing the British colonial regions
records.text:
Comparing the British colonial regions
Regions shared Atlantic trade, assemblies, and Anglicization but differed in labor, economy, and society because of environment and demography.
The British colonial regions shared a great deal. All exported goods across the Atlantic, all took part in the slave trade to some degree, all developed elected assemblies, and all became more English over time. They differed in environment, economy, labor, and society. The Chesapeake and plantation colonies grew cash crops using indentured servants and then enslaved Africans. New England built family farms, towns, and a mixed economy. The middle colonies exported grain and were the most diverse.
The explanations are largely environmental and demographic. Long growing seasons favored plantation crops and large enslaved workforces, rocky soil and short summers favored family farms and trade, and a rich grain belt and varied migration shaped the middle colonies.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 3
records.text:
Contextualizing Period 3
How the Seven Years' War, British imperial reform, colonial self-government, and Enlightenment ideas set the stage for independence and the first experiments in republican government, 1754–1800.
Period 3 begins with a war among empires and ends with a new republic, and each stage grew out of the conflict between imperial control and colonial self-government.
The CED asks you to explain the context in which America gained independence and developed a sense of national identity. For any Period 3 event, ask what came before it, what else was happening at the same time, and how both shaped it.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 3
records.heading: The colonies in 1754
records.text:
The colonies in 1754
A growing, self-governing set of colonies found itself in a contest with France and Native nations for the interior.
By 1754 the British colonies were growing quickly. They were tied to Britain by trade, print, and English political habits, and they governed themselves through elected assemblies. At the same time, the growing colonial population was expanding into the interior of North America, where it ran into French colonies and American Indian nations that depended on the fur trade and wanted to keep their lands.
The competition among the British, French, and American Indians for economic and political advantage culminated in the Seven Years' War (the French and Indian War), in which Britain defeated France and its Native allies. That victory is the starting point for nearly everything else in Period 3.
Context is the broader situation around an event, not the event itself. For the Revolution, the Seven Years' War and Britain's debts are context, while the Boston Tea Party is part of the story being explained.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 3
records.heading: Imperial control and self-government
records.text:
Imperial control and self-government
Tighter British control met colonial determination to govern themselves, and the clash led to independence.
British attempts to assert tighter control over its North American colonies and the colonial resolve to pursue self-government led to a colonial independence movement and the Revolutionary War. After 1763 Britain tried to raise revenue and manage its larger empire. Colonists who were used to governing themselves, and who drew on their rights as British subjects and on the ideas of the Enlightenment, resisted.
Protest moved from petitions and boycotts to armed conflict in 1775 and to a declaration of independence in 1776. The war that followed ended with British recognition of American independence in 1783.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 3
records.heading: Building a republic
records.text:
Building a republic
Revolutionary ideals led to new governments, new parties, and new conflicts over land, trade, and who counted as a citizen.
The American Revolution's democratic and republican ideals inspired new experiments with different forms of government. The states wrote new constitutions, the Articles of Confederation created a weak national government, and the Constitution of 1787 replaced it with a stronger one. In the 1790s disagreements among leaders produced the first political parties.
The new nation also faced conflict over land, borders, and trade. Migration within North America and competition over resources intensified conflicts among peoples and nations, and the continued presence of British and Spanish power challenged the United States to protect its borders and trade. Questions about slavery and the rights of women showed that the ideals of the Revolution were not applied to everyone.

records.title: The Seven Years’ War (The French and Indian War)
records.text:
The Seven Years’ War (The French and Indian War)
Why Britain and France went to war over the North American interior, how Britain won, and how victory left Britain in debt and set the stage for new imperial policies and colonial resentment.
The Seven Years' War removed France from eastern North America, but victory left Britain with debts and new responsibilities that led it to tighten control over the colonies.
The CED asks you to explain the causes and effects of the Seven Years' War. The war's most important effects were not on the battlefield but in the years after 1763, so keep asking what Britain and the colonists each wanted next.

records.title: The Seven Years’ War (The French and Indian War)
records.heading: Rivalry in the interior
records.text:
Rivalry in the interior
British expansion into the Ohio Valley threatened French and Native interests and brought on the war.
Colonial rivalry intensified between Britain and France in the mid-18th century as the growing population of the British colonies expanded into the interior of North America, threatening French–Indian trade networks and American Indian autonomy. The Ohio River Valley was the center of the dispute, because both empires claimed it and many Native nations lived and traded there.
The war began in 1754 with fighting in the Ohio Valley, where George Washington, then a young Virginia militia officer, was forced to surrender at Fort Necessity. In the same year, colonial delegates meeting at Albany considered Benjamin Franklin's plan for a union of the colonies, but no colony approved it. The French and their Native allies won early victories. The conflict then widened into a global war, called the Seven Years' War in Europe, and under the leadership of William Pitt, Britain committed money, ships, and soldiers to North America. Britain captured Quebec in 1759 and Montreal in 1760.

records.title: The Seven Years’ War (The French and Indian War)
records.heading: Victory at tremendous expense
records.text:
Victory at tremendous expense
Victory removed France but left Britain with debts and a larger empire, which led it to look to the colonies for revenue and control.
Britain achieved a major expansion of its territorial holdings by defeating the French, but at tremendous expense. In the Treaty of Paris of 1763, France gave up Canada and its claims east of the Mississippi River, and Spain, which had entered the war late on the French side, gave Florida to Britain. France had earlier transferred Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain.
Britain now ruled an enormous empire, owed a large debt, and needed troops to defend its new frontier. These conditions set the stage for imperial efforts to raise revenue and consolidate control over the colonies, which led to the conflicts described in Topic 3.3.
Colonists and British officials drew different lessons from the war. Many colonists believed they had helped win it and deserved more say, while many British officials believed the colonists had been defended at British expense and should help pay.

records.title: The Seven Years’ War (The French and Indian War)
records.heading: The Proclamation of 1763 and Native resistance
records.text:
The Proclamation of 1763 and Native resistance
British efforts to restrain western settlement angered colonists, while Native nations resisted settlers' advance.
After the British victory, imperial officials' attempts to prevent colonists from moving westward generated colonial opposition, while Native groups sought both to continue trading with Europeans and to resist the encroachments of colonists on tribal lands. In 1763, Native nations of the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley, inspired in part by the Ottawa leader Pontiac, attacked British forts, because they feared British settlement and disliked British trade policies.
The Crown responded with the Proclamation of 1763, which forbade colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains and reserved the western lands for Native peoples. Colonists who had expected to claim western land, including veterans and land speculators, resented the order, and many settlers moved west anyway. The line was hard to enforce and added to colonial opposition to British policy.

records.text:
Taxation Without Representation
How Parliament's efforts to raise revenue and assert authority after 1763 united the colonists in protest, what arguments they used, and how resistance moved from boycotts to war.
New taxes and controls imposed without colonial consent united colonists who defended their rights as British subjects and their traditions of self-rule.
The CED asks you to explain how British colonial policies regarding North America led to the Revolutionary War. For each policy, ask what Britain wanted, how colonists responded, and what the response showed about their ideas of rights.

records.title: Taxation Without Representation
records.heading: New taxes and controls, 1764–1775
records.text:
New taxes and controls, 1764–1775
After 1763 Parliament tried to raise revenue and tighten control, and each effort met colonial resistance that grew more organized.
New British efforts to collect taxes without direct colonial representation or consent, and to assert imperial authority in the colonies, began to unite the colonists against perceived and real constraints on their economic activities and political rights. The Sugar Act of 1764 taxed imported sugar and molasses and strengthened enforcement against smuggling. The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed printed materials such as newspapers, legal documents, and playing cards, and it was the first direct tax Parliament placed on the colonists.
Colonial protest, including the Stamp Act Congress and boycotts of British goods, led Parliament to repeal the Stamp Act in 1766. At the same time Parliament passed the Declaratory Act, which claimed the power to make laws for the colonies “in all cases whatsoever.” The Townshend Acts of 1767 placed duties on imports such as glass, paper, paint, and tea, and colonists responded with new boycotts. Most of those duties were repealed in 1770, but the tax on tea remained.
In March 1770 soldiers fired on a Boston crowd and killed five colonists in the Boston Massacre. The Tea Act of 1773 helped the East India Company sell tea cheaply in the colonies, but colonists saw it as a trick to make them accept Parliament's tax, and in December 1773 Bostonians dumped tea into the harbor. Parliament answered with the Coercive Acts of 1774, which closed Boston's port and limited self-government in Massachusetts and which colonists called the Intolerable Acts. The First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in 1774 and organized a boycott of British goods. In April 1775, fighting at Lexington and Concord began the war.

records.text: New British efforts to collect taxes without direct colonial representation or consent, and to assert imperial authority in the colonies, began to unite the colonists against perceived and real constraints on their economic activities and political rights. records.title: Taxation Without Representation
records.heading: Arguments for resistance
records.text:
Arguments for resistance
Colonists argued from the rights of British subjects, local self-rule, and Enlightenment ideas that only their own representatives could tax them.
Colonial leaders based their calls for resistance to Britain on arguments about the rights of British subjects, the rights of the individual, local traditions of self-rule, and the ideas of the Enlightenment. They argued that, as British subjects, they could be taxed only by representatives they had chosen, which gave rise to the slogan “no taxation without representation.” They pointed to their own assemblies, which had long taxed and governed the colonies.
British officials answered that Parliament represented all British subjects, including colonists who elected no members, a claim often called virtual representation. Many colonists rejected it. John Dickinson's Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania (1767–1768) argued that Parliament could regulate trade but could not tax the colonists to raise revenue. Colonists also drew on Locke's idea that governments exist to protect natural rights and on a tradition that warned that unchecked power tends to corrupt liberty.
“No taxation without representation” did not mean most colonists wanted seats in Parliament. Most wanted to be taxed only by their own assemblies.

records.title: Taxation Without Representation
records.heading: Popular movements and shared sacrifice
records.text:
Popular movements and shared sacrifice
Leaders, crowds, artisans, and women all took part in organized resistance, which gave the movement broad support.
The effort for American independence was energized by colonial leaders such as Benjamin Franklin, as well as by popular movements that included the political activism of laborers, artisans, and women. Franklin, who lived in London as a colonial agent, explained colonial objections to Parliament. In port cities, crowds known as the Sons of Liberty pressured stamp distributors to resign. Artisans and merchants joined boycotts, and women formed groups such as the Daughters of Liberty, who spun cloth at home and gave up British tea. Committees of correspondence, organized in the early 1770s, linked towns and colonies so that they could share news and coordinate resistance.
In the face of economic shortages and the British military occupation of some regions, men and women mobilized in large numbers to provide financial and material support to the Patriot movement. Women ran farms and shops while men served in the army, raised money, and made clothing for soldiers.

records.title: Philosophical Foundations of the American Revolution
records.text:
Philosophical Foundations of the American Revolution
The Enlightenment, religion, and republican ideas that shaped colonial attitudes toward government and the individual, and how Common Sense and the Declaration of Independence expressed them.
The ideals behind the Revolution grew out of new beliefs about politics, religion, and society that had been developing through the 18th century.
The CED asks you to explain how and why colonial attitudes about government and the individual changed before the Revolution. Pair each idea with a document or event where colonists put it to use, and note that these documents shaped later American ideals as well.
records.excerpt: The Enlightenment, religion, and republican ideas that shaped colonial attitudes toward government and the individual, and how Common Sense and the Declaration of Independence expressed them.

records.title: Philosophical Foundations of the American Revolution
records.heading: Enlightenment ideas and religion
records.text:
Enlightenment ideas and religion
Reason and natural rights, together with religious ideas of liberty, led colonists to value talent over birth and to question inherited authority.
Enlightenment ideas and philosophy inspired many American political thinkers to emphasize individual talent over hereditary privilege, while religion strengthened Americans' view of themselves as a people blessed with liberty. Enlightenment writers argued that reason could be used to understand nature and society and that government existed to serve people rather than the other way around. John Locke's argument that people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property, and that governments rest on the consent of the governed, had long been read in the colonies, and Montesquieu's ideas about dividing power among separate branches also influenced American thinkers.
Religion supported these ideas. The Great Awakening had taught many colonists to question established authority in matters of faith, and many ministers preached that Americans were a people blessed with liberty who should defend it. Both traditions encouraged colonists to value merit and conscience over birth and rank.

records.title: Philosophical Foundations of the American Revolution
records.heading: Republicanism and natural rights
records.text:
Republicanism and natural rights
Republicanism placed power in the people and their representatives and relied on civic virtue and fear of concentrated power.
The colonists' belief in the superiority of republican forms of government based on the natural rights of the people was central to the Revolutionary cause. In a republic, power comes from the people and is exercised by representatives, rather than being held by a monarch or a hereditary aristocracy. Republican thinkers believed that a republic depended on the civic virtue of its citizens, meaning their willingness to put the public good ahead of private interest, and they feared that power concentrated in a few hands would corrupt liberty.
These beliefs led colonists to see British actions after 1763 not only as unwise but as a threat to their liberty. They also helped explain why the new states chose republican governments rather than monarchies after independence.
A republic is not the same as a democracy. Revolutionary leaders wanted government by representatives chosen by the people, and many feared that unchecked popular majorities could also threaten liberty.
