records.title: Philosophical Foundations of the American Revolution
records.heading: Common Sense and the Declaration of Independence
records.text:
Common Sense and the Declaration of Independence
Common Sense and the Declaration turned republican and natural-rights ideas into a public case for independence that Americans would cite for generations.
The belief in republican government found expression in Thomas Paine's Common Sense and the Declaration of Independence. Paine's pamphlet, published in January 1776, attacked monarchy and hereditary rule, argued that it was absurd for a continent to be governed by an island, and called for independence in plain language that ordinary readers could follow. It was widely read and helped turn colonial opinion away from reconciliation with Britain.
The Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776. Thomas Jefferson was the principal author. The Declaration stated that all men are created equal and have unalienable rights, that governments derive their powers from the consent of the governed, and that people may change or abolish a government that violates those rights. It then listed grievances against King George III.
The ideas in these documents resonated throughout American history, shaping Americans' understanding of the ideals on which the nation was based. Later reformers appealed to the Declaration's language of equality and rights to demand that the nation live up to its principles.

records.title: The American Revolution
records.text:
The American Revolution
How the war began, the turning points that saved the Patriot cause, and why Britain's apparent advantages were not enough to defeat the colonies.
Despite loyalist opposition and Britain's apparent military and financial advantages, the Patriot cause succeeded because of the combined effects of the colonists' own efforts and help from abroad.
The CED asks you to explain how various factors contributed to the American victory. Be ready to rank the factors and to say why a single cause is not enough.

records.title: The American Revolution
records.heading: The war begins
records.text:
The war begins
The war began in Massachusetts in 1775, widened into a fight for independence by 1776, and divided colonists into Patriots and Loyalists.
Fighting began in April 1775 when British troops marching to seize colonial military supplies clashed with militia at Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts. The Second Continental Congress met in Philadelphia, created the Continental Army, and named George Washington its commander. In July 1775 Congress sent the Olive Branch Petition to the king, who rejected it, and in July 1776 Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence.
Not all colonists supported the Patriot cause. Loyalists, who stayed faithful to the Crown, were a substantial minority, and some regions, especially in the South and in parts of New York, were bitterly divided. The war was in part a civil war among colonists.

records.title: The American Revolution
records.heading: Turning points
records.text:
Turning points
Saratoga brought the French alliance, and the allied victory at Yorktown led to the Treaty of Paris of 1783.
After early defeats in 1776, Washington's surprise victory at Trenton at the end of the year lifted Patriot morale. The Patriot victory at Saratoga in New York in 1777 convinced France that the Americans could win. In 1778 France signed an alliance with the United States, and soon provided money, supplies, troops, and naval power. Spain and the Netherlands later joined the war against Britain, which turned the conflict into a wider European and global war.
The Continental Army endured the hard winter at Valley Forge in 1777–1778 and emerged better trained. After 1778 the British shifted their effort to the South, but they struggled to hold territory there. In 1781, a combined American and French army and French fleet trapped a British army under General Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, and he surrendered in October. The Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognized American independence and set the new nation's boundaries from the Atlantic to the Mississippi River.

records.title: The American Revolution
records.heading: Why the Patriots won
records.text:
Why the Patriots won
Colonial effort, leadership, commitment, and European help together overcame Britain's advantages.
The Patriot cause succeeded because of the actions of colonial militias and the Continental Army, George Washington's military leadership, the colonists' ideological commitment and resilience, and assistance sent by European allies. Washington kept the army together through defeat and hardship and avoided the destruction of his forces. Militias controlled their local areas and wore down British forces. Many Patriots remained committed to republican ideals even when the war went badly.
Britain faced its own problems. Its armies were thousands of miles from home, the colonies were too large to occupy, and British leaders could not win the support of enough colonists to hold the territory that their soldiers captured. French assistance, in money, equipment, soldiers, and sea power, was decisive at Yorktown.
Do not credit one cause alone. The French alliance mattered, but it came after Saratoga showed that the Patriots could fight, and it did not remove the need for Washington's army or local militias.

records.title: The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals
records.text:
The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals
How Revolutionary ideals of equality and liberty led some Americans to challenge slavery and expand political participation, how women's roles were redefined, and how the Revolution inspired movements abroad.
The Revolution's ideals made inequalities in American society harder to ignore, but they were applied unevenly and left slavery and many exclusions in place.
The CED asks you to explain the various ways the Revolution affected society and to describe its global impact. Look for both the change that Revolutionary ideals produced and the limits on that change.
records.excerpt: How Revolutionary ideals of equality and liberty led some Americans to challenge slavery and expand political participation, how women's roles were redefined, and how the Revolution inspired movements abroad.

records.title: The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals
records.heading: Equality, slavery, and political democracy
records.text:
Equality, slavery, and political democracy
The Revolution encouraged antislavery action and wider political participation, but both advanced unevenly.
During and after the American Revolution, an increased awareness of inequalities in society motivated some individuals and groups to call for the abolition of slavery and greater political democracy in the new state and national governments. Many Patriots saw a contradiction between demanding liberty from Britain and holding people in slavery. Quakers and other reformers led antislavery efforts, and enslaved and free Black Americans petitioned for freedom, used the courts, and some served in the Continental Army.
The result was uneven. Vermont's 1777 constitution banned slavery, Pennsylvania began gradual emancipation in 1780, and Massachusetts courts ended slavery in the state in the 1780s, while other northern states adopted gradual emancipation laws in the years that followed. Slavery remained central to the economy of the South. In 1775 Virginia's royal governor, Lord Dunmore, offered freedom to enslaved people who left rebel owners and joined the British, and thousands of enslaved people fled to British lines during the war.
Calls for greater political democracy also appeared in the new state governments. Some states widened participation, but property qualifications for voting remained common, and women and most free Black men could not vote in most states.

records.title: The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals
records.heading: Women and republican motherhood
records.text:
Women and republican motherhood
Republican motherhood gave women a civic role as teachers of republican values, without political equality.
Women contributed to the Revolutionary cause by boycotting British goods, running farms and businesses, raising money, nursing the wounded, and following the army. In response to women's participation in the American Revolution, Enlightenment ideas, and women's appeals for expanded roles, an ideal of “republican motherhood” gained popularity. It called on women to teach republican values within the family and granted women a new importance in American political culture.
Abigail Adams, writing to her husband John Adams while he served in Congress in 1776, urged him to consider women's legal position as the new government was shaped. The ideal of republican motherhood gave women a recognized civic role and encouraged the education of girls, but it did not give women the vote or equal legal rights.
Republican motherhood expanded women's civic importance without giving women political rights. It placed women's political role within the home.

records.title: The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals
records.heading: The global impact of the Revolution
records.text:
The global impact of the Revolution
The Revolution's ideals helped inspire later independence movements in France, Haiti, and Latin America.
The American Revolution and the ideals set forth in the Declaration of Independence reverberated in France, Haiti, and Latin America, inspiring future independence movements. In France, the American example and ideas about natural rights and popular government helped inspire revolutionaries in 1789. In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, an uprising by enslaved people that began in 1791 led to the independent Republic of Haiti in 1804. In the early 1800s, independence movements spread across Spanish and Portuguese America.
Each of these movements had its own causes and its own leaders, so the American Revolution is best seen as one important influence among several.

State constitutions gave the most power to legislatures, limited governors, and protected rights.

records.title: The Articles of Confederation
records.heading: The Articles of Confederation
records.text:
The Articles of Confederation
The Articles preserved state power and won the war, but a government without the power to tax or regulate trade could not solve postwar problems.
The Articles of Confederation unified the newly independent states, creating a central government with limited power. Congress was the only branch of the national government. Each state had one vote, there was no president, and the national government had no power to tax or to regulate trade among the states. Important laws required the approval of nine of the thirteen states, and changing the Articles required the agreement of all thirteen. The Articles were adopted by Congress in 1777 and went into force in 1781 after all the states had ratified them.
The new government won the war and negotiated the Treaty of Paris of 1783. After the Revolution, however, difficulties over international trade, finances, interstate commerce, foreign relations, and internal unrest led to calls for a stronger central government. Congress had to ask the states for money and could not make them pay. States set up trade barriers against one another, Britain refused to leave forts in the Northwest, and Spain closed the Mississippi River to American navigation in 1784, hurting western settlers.
In 1786–1787, Shays' Rebellion, in which indebted farmers in western Massachusetts shut down courts to stop foreclosures, frightened many leaders. The national government had no army to put down the rebellion and the state had to raise a militia on its own. To many Americans, the episode showed the need for a government able to keep order.

records.title: The Articles of Confederation
records.heading: Settling the West
records.text:
Settling the West
The Northwest Ordinance created a lasting model for admitting new states and banned slavery in the Northwest Territory.
As settlers moved westward during the 1780s, Congress enacted the Northwest Ordinance for admitting new states. The Land Ordinance of 1785 set up a system for surveying and selling western land in orderly townships and set aside land for public schools. The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 provided for governing the territory north of the Ohio River and a path to statehood on equal terms with the original states once a territory reached a certain population. The ordinance promoted public education, the protection of private property, and a ban on slavery in the Northwest Territory.
These laws were among the most lasting achievements of the Confederation Congress, and they created a model for how the nation would expand. They did not recognize the land claims of the Native peoples who lived in the region, which led to conflict.

records.title: The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification
records.heading: The Convention and its compromises
records.text:
The Convention and its compromises
Compromises over representation and slavery made the Constitution possible, and the compromises over slavery gave the institution protection.
In the summer of 1787, delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia, with Rhode Island absent, and through negotiation, collaboration, and compromise proposed a constitution. They had been called to revise the Articles of Confederation, but they wrote a new plan of government. George Washington presided, and James Madison's notes are the most complete record of the debates.
The delegates first disagreed over representation. The Virginia Plan, supported by large states, called for a strong national government with representation based on population. The New Jersey Plan, supported by small states, called for a single house of Congress with equal representation for each state. The Great Compromise created a House of Representatives based on population and a Senate with two members from each state.
The delegates also compromised over the representation of slave states in Congress and the role of the federal government in regulating both slavery and the slave trade. Under the Three-Fifths Compromise, three-fifths of the enslaved population would be counted for representation and direct taxes. The Constitution allowed the prohibition of the international slave trade after 1808, and it required the return of people who escaped slavery. Delegates from the Deep South made clear that they would not join the new government without such protections, and the compromises gave slavery a protected place in the new government.

records.title: The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification
records.heading: Federalists and Anti-Federalists
records.text:
Federalists and Anti-Federalists
Federalists argued that a large republic with divided power would protect liberty, while Anti-Federalists feared distant, powerful government.
When the Constitution was sent to the states for ratification, Anti-Federalists opposing ratification battled with Federalists, whose principles were articulated in the Federalist Papers, primarily written by Alexander Hamilton and James Madison, with John Jay. Federalists argued that a stronger national government was needed to govern a large country and that the new system would protect liberty by dividing power. In Federalist No. 10, Madison argued that a large republic would make it harder for a single faction to control the government, because there would be many competing interests.
Anti-Federalists, among them Patrick Henry and George Mason, feared that a distant national government would threaten the rights of individuals and the powers of the states. Many believed that republics worked best in small communities where representatives stayed close to the people. They also objected that the Constitution had no bill of rights.
Nine states had to approve the Constitution for it to take effect. Delaware ratified first, in December 1787, and New Hampshire became the ninth state in June 1788. The large states of Virginia and New York ratified after bitter debates.

records.title: The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification
records.heading: The Bill of Rights
records.text:
The Bill of Rights
The promise of a Bill of Rights secured ratification, and the first ten amendments limited the powers of the federal government.
Federalists ensured the ratification of the Constitution by promising the addition of a Bill of Rights that enumerated individual rights and explicitly restricted the powers of the federal government. Several states ratified with recommended amendments. In 1789 the First Congress, led by James Madison, proposed amendments, and ten of them were ratified in 1791. They protected freedom of religion, speech, press, and assembly, the right to bear arms, rights of the accused such as trial by jury, and reserved to the states and the people the powers not given to the federal government.
The Bill of Rights answered a central Anti-Federalist objection and made the new government more acceptable to those who feared central power.
The Bill of Rights was not part of the Constitution as signed in 1787. It was added after ratification, as the price of winning support.

records.text:
The Constitution
How the Constitution created a limited but dynamic national government through federalism and the separation of powers, and what it kept and changed from the Articles and from colonial government.
The Constitution created a limited but dynamic central government that embodied federalism and provided for a separation of powers among three branches.
The CED asks you to explain continuities and changes in the structure and functions of government with ratification of the Constitution. For each feature, ask what it kept from earlier governments and what it changed.

records.title: The Constitution
records.heading: Federalism
records.text:
Federalism
Federalism shares power between the national and state governments and gives the national government specific powers, including taxation and the regulation of commerce.
Delegates from the states participated in the Constitutional Convention that created a limited but dynamic central government embodying federalism. Federalism divides power between the national government and the states. The Constitution gave Congress specific powers, which are called enumerated powers. Article I, Section 8 included the power to lay and collect taxes, to borrow money, and to regulate commerce with foreign nations, among the states, and with the Indian tribes. It also gave Congress the power to make all laws “necessary and proper” to carry out those powers, a clause that allowed the national government to grow in later years.
The Constitution declared itself the supreme law of the land, which meant that valid federal law overrode conflicting state law. Powers not given to the national government remained with the states or the people, a principle later stated in the Tenth Amendment. States kept responsibility for much of daily life, including most criminal law, education, and local government.

records.title: The Constitution
records.heading: Separation of powers and checks and balances
records.text:
Separation of powers and checks and balances
Three branches with checks on one another limit the power of each, and indirect election limited the influence of popular majorities.
The Constitution provided for a separation of powers among three branches. Congress, which makes laws, is divided into a House of Representatives and a Senate. The president, who carries out the laws, is chosen by an Electoral College, and the federal courts interpret the law. Each branch can check the others. The president can veto bills, Congress can override a veto and can impeach officials, the Senate approves treaties and appointments, including federal judges, and the courts decide cases under the Constitution and federal law.
These arrangements reflected the fear of concentrated power that Revolutionary leaders had learned from republican thinkers and from Montesquieu. They also limited excessive popular influence. Senators were chosen by state legislatures and presidents were chosen by electors rather than by direct vote, so only the House was elected directly by voters.
The process of amending the Constitution was made difficult but not impossible, which allowed it to change over time.

records.title: The Constitution
records.heading: Continuities and changes from the Articles
records.text:
Continuities and changes from the Articles
The Constitution kept the republic and the states but gave the national government the structure and powers that the Articles had lacked.
The Constitution kept the republican form of government, the written framework, the states, and a Congress, and it kept many familiar features of colonial and state government, such as elected legislatures with two houses and a division of powers. The Constitution changed the structure of the national government. It created an executive and a national court system, gave the national government direct power to tax and to regulate commerce among the states, provided that federal law was supreme over state law, and replaced one vote per state with representation in the House based on population.
Ratification therefore preserved the republican ideals of the Revolution while correcting the weaknesses that the Articles had shown. Its supporters considered it a stronger government that nonetheless remained limited by law.
The Constitution did not abolish state governments. It created a stronger national government on top of state governments that kept real power.

records.title: Shaping a New Republic
records.text:
Shaping a New Republic
How Washington and Adams put the Constitution into practice, why disputes over economics and foreign policy produced the first political parties, and how the new nation dealt with Britain, Spain, France, and American Indian nations.
In the 1790s the new government built lasting institutions, and disagreements over the nation's economy, foreign policy, and the meaning of the Constitution gave rise to political parties.
The CED asks you to explain how competition intensified conflicts among peoples and nations and how political ideas, institutions, and party systems developed. Keep the domestic and the foreign sides together, because the French Revolution drove both.

records.title: Shaping a New Republic
records.heading: Washington, Adams, and institutions
records.text:
Washington, Adams, and institutions
Washington and Adams made the Constitution work by creating departments, courts, a financial system, and precedents.
During the presidential administrations of George Washington and John Adams, political leaders created institutions and precedents that put the principles of the Constitution into practice. Washington took office in 1789. He appointed department heads, including Alexander Hamilton as Secretary of the Treasury and Thomas Jefferson as Secretary of State, who met with him as a cabinet. The Judiciary Act of 1789 established the federal court system.
Hamilton proposed a financial program to strengthen the national government and its credit. It called for the federal government to pay the national debt and to assume the states' war debts, to create a national bank, and to raise revenue through tariffs and an excise tax on whiskey. His supporters saw a program that would build the nation's economy, while opponents saw a program that favored merchants and speculators and expanded federal power. In 1794 farmers in western Pennsylvania resisted the whiskey tax in the Whiskey Rebellion, and Washington led a large militia force to the region, which demonstrated that the federal government could enforce its laws.
Washington's Farewell Address, published in 1796, encouraged national unity, as he cautioned against political factions and warned about the danger of permanent foreign alliances. Washington decided not to seek a third term, setting a precedent that lasted more than a century.

records.title: Shaping a New Republic
records.heading: Parties and foreign policy
records.text:
Parties and foreign policy
Disputes over the national government's power, the economy, and the French Revolution divided leaders into the first two political parties.
Political leaders in the 1790s took a variety of positions on issues such as the relationship between the national government and the states, economic policy, foreign policy, and the balance between liberty and order. This led to the formation of political parties, most significantly the Federalists, led by Alexander Hamilton, and the Democratic-Republican Party, led by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. Federalists favored a strong national government, commerce and manufacturing, and friendly ties with Britain. Democratic-Republicans favored limited national government, a strict reading of the Constitution, agriculture, and sympathy for France.
War between France and Britain resulting from the French Revolution presented challenges to the United States over issues of free trade and foreign policy and fostered political disagreement. Washington issued a Neutrality Proclamation in 1793, but Britain seized American ships and sailors. Jay's Treaty of 1794 settled some disputes and led Britain to remove troops from forts in the Northwest, but it was unpopular with Democratic-Republicans, who thought it favored Britain. Under Pinckney's Treaty of 1795, Spain recognized American rights to navigate the Mississippi River and to store goods at New Orleans, and settled the southern boundary.
Under President Adams, relations with France worsened. In the XYZ Affair, French agents demanded bribes from American diplomats, and an undeclared naval conflict called the Quasi-War followed. The Federalist Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts in 1798, which lengthened the residency required for citizenship, allowed the president to deport noncitizens judged dangerous, and made it a crime to publish false or malicious statements against the government. Democratic-Republicans saw the laws as attacks on their party and on freedom of speech. Jefferson and Madison replied with the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions, which argued that states could judge the constitutionality of federal laws.
Washington warned against political parties, yet the parties formed during his own presidency. Do not treat the Farewell Address as describing a world without parties.

records.title: Shaping a New Republic
records.heading: Borders, American Indians, and Spanish California
records.text:
Borders, American Indians, and Spanish California
The United States used treaties and force to secure its borders and the Ohio country, while Spain expanded missions in California.
The U.S. government forged diplomatic initiatives aimed at dealing with the continued British and Spanish presence in North America, as U.S. settlers migrated beyond the Appalachians and sought free navigation of the Mississippi River. Pinckney's Treaty addressed the Mississippi question, and Jay's Treaty addressed the British forts.
An ambiguous relationship between the federal government and American Indian tribes contributed to problems regarding treaties and American Indian legal claims relating to the seizure of their lands. The Constitution gave Congress authority over commerce with the tribes, and the government made treaties with them, but states, settlers, and speculators often ignored those agreements. After a Native confederacy in the Ohio country defeated U.S. armies in the early 1790s, General Anthony Wayne defeated it at Fallen Timbers in 1794, and in the Treaty of Greenville of 1795 the tribes gave up much of present-day Ohio.
In the West, the Spanish, supported by the bonded labor of the local American Indians, expanded their mission settlements into California. These missions provided opportunities for social mobility for soldiers and led to new cultural blending, even as Native people suffered from disease and forced labor.

records.title: Developing an American Identity
records.text:
Developing an American Identity
How Americans expressed a national identity after the Revolution in language, literature, art, and architecture, while regional differences continued.
Americans began to create a national culture that expressed republican ideals, but regional differences continued.
The CED asks you to explain the continuities and changes in American culture from 1754 to 1800. This topic is a development topic, so aim to describe a change and explain why it happened.

records.title: Developing an American Identity
records.heading: A new national culture
records.text:
A new national culture
After independence, Americans promoted a distinct national culture through language, education, symbols, and religious freedom.
New forms of national culture developed in the United States alongside continued regional variations. After independence, writers, artists, and educators saw a need to establish a distinctive American culture to match the new republic. Noah Webster's spelling book and later dictionary promoted a standard American usage of English, and school texts taught republican virtue and love of country. Americans celebrated Washington as a national hero, and the symbols of the new nation, including the eagle and the flag, spread.
Many people believed that republican government required an educated citizenry, so there was new attention to schools and to the education of both boys and girls. Americans also dropped many traditional ties to Britain. Several states ended official support for churches, and Virginia's Statute for Religious Freedom (1786) separated church and state.

records.title: Developing an American Identity
records.heading: Art, literature, and architecture
records.text:
Art, literature, and architecture
Painters, writers, and architects used American subjects and classical models to express national identity.
Ideas about national identity increasingly found expression in works of art, literature, and architecture. Painters such as Charles Willson Peale and Gilbert Stuart made portraits of Revolutionary leaders, and John Trumbull painted scenes from the Revolution. Writers such as Royall Tyler, whose play The Contrast (1787) contrasted American simplicity with European manners, and Philip Freneau, whose poetry celebrated the Revolution, tried to create a literature with American themes. Phillis Wheatley, an enslaved woman who published poetry in the 1770s, showed that Black writers also took part in this culture.
In architecture, Americans favored a neoclassical style drawing on Greek and Roman models, which they associated with republican government. Thomas Jefferson's design for the Virginia state capitol and his own home, Monticello, are examples, and the new capital city of Washington, D.C., was planned with large public buildings in this style.

records.title: Developing an American Identity
records.heading: Regional variations
records.text:
Regional variations
National identity grew while regional differences in economy, society, and politics continued.
A national culture did not erase regional differences. New England had towns centered on churches and commerce, the Middle Atlantic region had a diverse population and active trade, the South depended on plantation agriculture and slavery, and the backcountry had its own frontier culture. These regions differed over economic, political, social, and foreign policy issues, as the disputes between Federalists and Democratic-Republicans showed.
National identity and regional identity developed side by side, and the tension between them would shape American politics in the decades that followed.

records.title: Movement in the Early Republic
records.text:
Movement in the Early Republic
How American Indian nations adjusted their alliances, how westward migration spread frontier cultures and tensions, and how slavery expanded in the Deep South while antislavery sentiment grew in the North.
Movement of people into the interior intensified competition for land, and the growth of slavery in one region and its decline in another created lasting regional differences.
The CED asks you to explain how migration and immigration caused competition and conflict, and how regional attitudes about slavery changed. This topic builds connections across regions, so practice linking a cause to a pattern.

records.title: Movement in the Early Republic
records.heading: American Indian alliances
records.text:
American Indian alliances
Native nations made shifting alliances to protect their lands, and British support for them added to tensions with the United States.
Various American Indian groups repeatedly evaluated and adjusted their alliances with Europeans, other tribes, and the United States, seeking to limit migration of white settlers and maintain control of tribal lands and natural resources. During the Revolution, Native nations had to choose sides or try to stay neutral, and the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy split, with some nations supporting the Patriots and others the British. The Treaty of Paris of 1783 gave the United States land claimed by Native nations, who were not parties to it.
After the war, a confederation of Native peoples in the Ohio country resisted U.S. expansion with British support. British alliances with American Indians contributed to tensions between the United States and Britain, because British forts remained in the Northwest. These tensions eased after Fallen Timbers in 1794, when Native forces were defeated, and after Jay's Treaty, in which Britain agreed to leave the forts.

records.title: Movement in the Early Republic
records.heading: Westward migration and frontier cultures
records.text:
Westward migration and frontier cultures
Settlers who moved west brought frontier cultures with them and competed for land with Native peoples and one another.
As increasing numbers of migrants from North America and other parts of the world continued to move westward, frontier cultures that had emerged in the colonial period continued to grow, fueling social, political, and ethnic tensions. After the Revolution, settlers crossed the Appalachians into Kentucky and Tennessee, which became states in 1792 and 1796, and into the Ohio country. Many of them were of Scots-Irish and German descent, and they made their living from farming, hunting, and trade.
Frontier settlers wanted secure land titles, protection from Native peoples, and access to markets, especially through the Mississippi River. They often resented eastern elites and federal policies such as taxes, which was the background of the Whiskey Rebellion. Competition for land also meant conflict with Native nations, with the Spanish and British, and among settlers themselves.

records.title: Movement in the Early Republic
records.heading: Slavery and regional attitudes
records.text:
Slavery and regional attitudes
Slavery declined in the North and expanded in the Deep South, which created distinct regional attitudes.
The expansion of slavery in the Deep South and adjacent western lands and rising antislavery sentiment began to create distinctive regional attitudes toward slavery. In the North, states abolished slavery or adopted gradual emancipation, and the Northwest Ordinance banned slavery north of the Ohio River. Free Black communities in northern cities formed churches and aid societies, such as the Free African Society, founded in Philadelphia in 1787 by Richard Allen and Absalom Jones.
In the South, the invention of the cotton gin in 1793 made short-staple cotton profitable and encouraged the spread of slavery into the Deep South and westward. Many white Southerners who had once called slavery an evil came to defend it as necessary. The Constitution protected slavery with the Three-Fifths Compromise, the fugitive slave clause, and the delay of any ban on the international slave trade until 1808. Fear of slave rebellion, heightened by the Haitian Revolution, led Southern states to tighten control of enslaved people.
Slavery was not limited to the South in 1790, and antislavery action was not limited to the North. The pattern was uneven, and it was moving in different directions in different regions.

records.title: Continuity and Change in Period 3
records.text:
Continuity and Change in Period 3
A guide to describing and explaining what stayed the same and what changed in American politics, society, and ideas between 1754 and 1800.
Independence changed who governed and how, but many social patterns, including slavery and inequality, continued.
The CED treats continuity and change as a historical reasoning process. The strongest answers say what stayed the same, what changed, and why, using a specific example for each claim.

records.title: Continuity and Change in Period 3
records.heading: How to reason about continuity and change
records.text:
How to reason about continuity and change
Compare a category at the beginning and the end of the period, and explain the causes of change and the reasons for continuity.
Continuity and change over time means describing what remained the same and what shifted across a period, and explaining why. Start by choosing a starting point and an ending point. For Period 3, those are the colonial situation in 1754 and the new republic in 1800. Then pick a category, such as government, society, or ideas, and describe the state of that category at each end.
A claim about change should name the change, give evidence for it, and explain what caused it. A claim about continuity should name what persisted and explain why it persisted. Strong answers avoid treating a period as all change or all continuity.

records.title: Continuity and Change in Period 3
records.heading: Continuity and change in politics and government
records.text:
Continuity and change in politics and government
Government changed from monarchy to republic, but self-government traditions and debates over central power continued.
The independence movement changed the form of government. Colonists who had been subjects of a monarch built republics, wrote state constitutions and a federal Constitution, and formed political parties. Power moved from Parliament and the Crown to elected American governments, and the Constitution replaced the weak Articles with a stronger national government.
At the same time, much continued. Colonial assemblies became state legislatures, and traditions of local self-government, English legal rights, and fear of concentrated power continued from the colonial period. Property qualifications for voting remained common. Disputes between those who wanted a stronger central government and those who favored local and state power continued from the Articles to the Constitution to the parties of the 1790s.

records.title: Continuity and Change in Period 3
records.heading: Continuity and change in society and ideas
records.text:
Continuity and change in society and ideas
The Revolution changed ideas and some institutions, but slavery, inequality, and Native dispossession continued.
The American independence movement affected society in several ways. Revolutionary ideals led some Americans to challenge slavery, widened women's civic role through republican motherhood, and encouraged a national culture. Northern states ended or began to end slavery, and religious freedom expanded.
Yet slavery continued and grew in the South, women and most free Black men could not vote, and American Indian nations lost land as settlers moved west. The same Revolution that inspired antislavery arguments also left slavery protected in the Constitution. A balanced answer explains both the change and its limits.
Do not say the Revolution changed nothing or everything. Name the specific change, name what stayed the same, and say why.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 4
records.text:
Contextualizing Period 4
The context for Period 4: a more participatory democracy and a new national culture, an economy transformed by innovation, and a nation that expanded westward and argued over slavery, 1800–1848.
Between 1800 and 1848 the United States grew more democratic, more commercial, and larger, and each change raised new questions about who belonged in the nation and where slavery would be allowed.
The CED asks you to explain the context in which the republic developed from 1800 to 1848. For any Period 4 event, ask what the nation had inherited from the 1790s, what else was changing at the same time, and how both shaped the event.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 4
records.heading: Democracy and a national culture
records.text:
Democracy and a national culture
Suffrage grew for white men, parties multiplied, and a national culture and many reform movements developed.
The United States began to develop a modern democracy and celebrated a new national culture, while Americans sought to define the nation's democratic ideals and change their society and institutions to match them. The nation's transition to a more participatory democracy was achieved by expanding suffrage from a system based on property ownership to one based on voting by all adult white men, and it was accompanied by the growth of political parties.
While Americans embraced a new national culture, various groups developed distinctive cultures of their own. Increasing numbers of Americans, many inspired by new religious and intellectual movements, worked primarily outside of government institutions to advance their ideals, which led to reform movements such as temperance, abolitionism, and women's rights.
More participatory democracy did not mean democracy for everyone. In this period the vote expanded for white men while women, most African Americans, and American Indians stayed outside it.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 4
records.heading: Innovation and the market revolution
records.text:
Innovation and the market revolution
New technology and transportation expanded the economy, changed daily life, and drew regions together in some ways while setting them apart in others.
Innovations in technology, agriculture, and commerce powerfully accelerated the American economy, precipitating profound changes to U.S. society and to national and regional identities. New transportation systems and technologies, including canals, steamboats, and railroads, dramatically expanded manufacturing and agricultural production.
The changes caused by the market revolution had significant effects on U.S. society, workers' lives, and gender and family relations. Economic development shaped settlement and trade patterns, helping to unify the nation while also encouraging the growth of different regions.

records.title: Contextualizing Period 4
records.heading: Expansion, foreign policy, and slavery
records.text:
Expansion, foreign policy, and slavery
A growing nation claimed more territory, and each acquisition renewed the conflict over slavery.
The U.S. interest in increasing foreign trade and expanding its national borders shaped the nation's foreign policy and spurred government and private initiatives. Struggling to create an independent global presence, the United States sought to claim territory throughout the North American continent and promote foreign trade.
The United States' acquisition of lands in the West gave rise to contests over the extension of slavery into new territories. Each new addition of land raised the question of whether slavery would be allowed to spread, and that question would increasingly divide the nation.

records.title: The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson
records.text:
The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson
How the election of 1800, Jefferson's presidency, the Supreme Court's early decisions, and the Louisiana Purchase shaped national politics and the nation's reach across North America.
The early 1800s kept the party conflict of the 1790s alive, while the Supreme Court defined the Constitution's meaning and the Louisiana Purchase doubled the nation's size.
The CED asks you to explain the causes and effects of policy debates in the early republic. For each debate, ask which party took which side and what the outcome showed about the powers of the federal government.

records.title: The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson
records.heading: The election of 1800 and Jeffersonian politics
records.text:
The election of 1800 and Jeffersonian politics
The peaceful transfer of power in 1800 showed that the republic could survive party conflict, and foreign policy remained divisive.
In the early 1800s, national political parties continued to debate issues such as the tariff, the powers of the federal government, and relations with European powers. The election of 1800 was bitter. Thomas Jefferson, the Democratic-Republican candidate, tied in the Electoral College with his running mate, Aaron Burr, and the House of Representatives chose Jefferson as president. The Twelfth Amendment (1804) changed the Constitution so that electors would vote separately for president and vice president. The transfer of power from the Federalists to the Democratic-Republicans took place without violence.
In his First Inaugural Address, Jefferson tried to calm party feelings by saying, “We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.” His administration cut federal spending and taxes, including the excise tax on whiskey, and worked to reduce the national debt. Relations with European powers remained a problem. Britain and France seized American ships during their wars, and in 1807 Jefferson persuaded Congress to pass the Embargo Act, which forbade American ships to sail to foreign ports. The embargo hurt American merchants and was repealed in 1809.

records.title: The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson
records.heading: The Supreme Court and the Constitution
records.text:
The Supreme Court and the Constitution
The Marshall Court claimed the final word on the Constitution and strengthened federal power over the states.
Supreme Court decisions established the primacy of the judiciary in determining the meaning of the Constitution and asserted that federal laws took precedence over state laws. In Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall wrote that the Court had the power to decide whether a law passed by Congress was constitutional, which is known as judicial review. The case arose from the last-minute appointment of federal judges by the Federalists in 1801.
In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Court upheld Congress's power to charter a national bank and ruled that a state could not tax it, which established that federal law is supreme over state law. In Gibbons v. Ogden (1824), the Court held that the power to regulate interstate commerce belonged to Congress, which strengthened national authority over the economy.
Marbury v. Madison did not give the Court the power to make laws. It established that the Court could say what the Constitution means and could decide that an act of Congress violates it.

records.heading: The Louisiana Purchase and exploration
records.text:
The Louisiana Purchase and exploration
The purchase doubled the nation's size, and exploration helped establish American claims across the continent.
Following the Louisiana Purchase, the U.S. government sought influence and control over North America through a variety of means, including exploration and diplomatic efforts. In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France for about $15 million, which doubled the size of the nation. Jefferson had been unsure whether the Constitution allowed such a purchase, but he agreed because it gave American farmers access to the Mississippi River and the port of New Orleans and removed a European power from the western border.
Jefferson sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to explore the new territory and the lands beyond it. Their expedition, from 1804 to 1806, was guided in part by the Shoshone woman Sacagawea. It mapped routes to the Pacific, gathered information about the region's geography and peoples, and strengthened American claims to the Northwest.

records.title: Politics and Regional Interests
records.text:
Politics and Regional Interests
How the economic interests of the Northeast, South, and West shaped political positions in the 1810s and 1820s, how the American System aimed to unify the economy, and how the Missouri Compromise postponed the conflict over slavery.
Regional interests often trumped national concerns, and attempts to unify the economy and settle the question of slavery's expansion produced debates that deepened sectional differences.
The CED asks you to explain how different regional interests affected debates about the role of the federal government. Ask which region gained or lost under each policy and how that shaped its representatives' votes.

records.title: Politics and Regional Interests
records.heading: Regional interests and national politics
records.text:
Regional interests and national politics
The North, South, and West had different economic interests, and leaders voted according to those interests more than any national plan.
Regional interests often trumped national concerns as the basis for many political leaders' positions on slavery and economic policy. The Northeast had growing manufacturing and trade and wanted protection for its industries. The South depended on exporting cotton and other crops, bought manufactured goods, and generally opposed taxes that raised prices. The West wanted cheap land, access to markets, and roads and canals to carry its crops.
After the War of 1812 the Federalist Party collapsed, and the single-party politics of the Era of Good Feelings (about 1817–1825) hid sharp regional disputes within the Democratic-Republican Party. Without two parties to organize national debate, regional blocs competed within one party.

records.title: Politics and Regional Interests
records.heading: The American System
records.text:
The American System
The American System aimed to bind the nation's economy together, but it favored some regions more than others and raised constitutional questions.
Plans to further unify the U.S. economy, such as the American System, generated debates over whether such policies would benefit agriculture or industry, potentially favoring different sections of the country. Henry Clay of Kentucky promoted the American System, which called for a protective tariff to shelter American manufacturers from British competition, a national bank to provide a stable currency and credit, and federal spending on internal improvements such as roads and canals.
Congress passed the Tariff of 1816 and chartered the Second Bank of the United States in 1816. Supporters said the plan would knit the sections together by creating a national market, while opponents, especially in the South, said that tariffs raised the cost of manufactured goods and benefited the North, and many questioned whether the Constitution allowed the federal government to build roads and canals. Presidents Madison and Monroe vetoed bills for internal improvements on constitutional grounds, so such projects were often left to the states or private companies.

records.title: Politics and Regional Interests
records.heading: The Missouri Compromise
records.text:
The Missouri Compromise
The compromise preserved the Senate balance and drew a line across the Louisiana Purchase, but it postponed the conflict rather than ending it.
Congressional attempts at political compromise, such as the Missouri Compromise, only temporarily stemmed growing tensions between opponents and defenders of slavery. When Missouri asked to join the Union as a slave state in 1819, Representative James Tallmadge of New York proposed to restrict slavery there. Southerners objected because the balance between free and slave states in the Senate was at stake, and the Senate was equally divided.
In the compromise of 1820–1821, Maine entered as a free state and Missouri as a slave state, which kept the Senate balanced. Slavery was banned in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of the latitude 36°30′, except in Missouri. The agreement settled the immediate dispute but showed that Americans were dividing along sectional lines over slavery, and the question returned with each new territory.
The Missouri Compromise did not end slavery's expansion or the debate over it. It set a rule for one region and postponed the larger question.

America on the World Stage
How the War of 1812, border agreements with Britain and Spain, and the Monroe Doctrine expressed a growing American effort to claim territory, protect trade, and assert influence in the Western Hemisphere.
The United States tried to create an independent global presence by claiming territory across the continent, defending its trade, and warning European powers away from the Western Hemisphere.
The CED asks you to explain how and why American foreign policy developed and expanded. Pair each action with its aim: security, trade, or territory.

records.title: America on the World Stage
records.heading: The War of 1812
records.text:
The War of 1812
The war grew out of conflicts over trade and the frontier, and it ended in a draw that strengthened national feeling and weakened Native resistance.
Struggling to create an independent global presence, the United States sought to claim territory throughout the North American continent and promote foreign trade. Britain and France continued to interfere with American shipping in their wars, and Britain impressed sailors from American ships, which angered many Americans. In the West, settlers blamed the British for supporting Native resistance. The Shawnee leader Tecumseh and his brother Tenskwatawa built a confederacy of Native nations to resist the loss of land, and U.S. forces under William Henry Harrison defeated them at Tippecanoe in 1811.
A group of young congressmen from the South and West, called War Hawks, pushed for war, and Congress declared war on Britain in June 1812. The fighting included the British burning of Washington in 1814, the defense of Baltimore that inspired the “Star-Spangled Banner,” and Andrew Jackson's victory at New Orleans in January 1815, which took place after the peace treaty had been signed at Ghent in December 1814. The treaty restored the situation before the war.
The war's effects were large even though it ended without territorial change. It strengthened national feeling, weakened the Federalist Party after its Hartford Convention criticized the war, destroyed Tecumseh's confederacy and weakened Native resistance east of the Mississippi, and encouraged American manufacturing by cutting off British imports.

records.heading: Diplomacy and borders
records.text:
Diplomacy and borders
Treaties with Britain and Spain fixed the northern boundary, gave the United States Florida, and extended its claims to the Pacific.
After the war the United States settled its borders through diplomacy. The Rush–Bagot Agreement of 1817 limited naval forces on the Great Lakes, and the Convention of 1818 set the northern boundary between the Louisiana Purchase and British Canada at the 49th parallel and provided for joint American and British occupation of the Oregon Country.
In the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819, Spain gave Florida to the United States and accepted a boundary that ran to the Pacific, which gave the United States a claim on the Pacific coast. These agreements reduced the British and Spanish presence on the nation's borders without war.

records.title: America on the World Stage
records.heading: The Monroe Doctrine
records.text:
The Monroe Doctrine
The Monroe Doctrine warned Europe against intervening in the Western Hemisphere, and it later became a foundation of American foreign policy.
The U.S. government sought influence and control over the Western Hemisphere through a variety of means, including military actions, American Indian removal, and diplomatic efforts such as the Monroe Doctrine. In the 1810s and 1820s, most of Spain's colonies in Latin America won independence, and European monarchies talked of helping Spain regain them. Britain, which wanted to keep trade with the new nations, proposed a joint statement, but Secretary of State John Quincy Adams urged the United States to act on its own.
In his annual message of December 1823, President James Monroe declared that the United States would regard any attempt by a European power to extend its system to any part of the Western Hemisphere as dangerous to the nation's peace and safety. He also said that the United States would not interfere with existing European colonies and would not take part in European wars. The Monroe Doctrine had little force at the time, because the United States lacked the strength to enforce it, and British naval power protected the new nations. Later presidents invoked it to justify American influence in the hemisphere.
The Monroe Doctrine was a statement of policy and not a treaty or an alliance. In 1823 it was effective mainly because Britain's navy also opposed European intervention.

records.title: Market Revolution: Industrialization
records.text:
Market Revolution: Industrialization
How entrepreneurs, new machines, and new transportation networks created a market revolution between 1800 and 1848, and why the North, the Midwest, and the South were linked in different ways.
New machines, new roads, canals, and railroads, and government support for them created a market economy, and that economy tied the North and Midwest together while binding the South to cotton exports.
The CED asks you to explain the causes and effects of innovations in technology, agriculture, and commerce. For each innovation, ask what it made cheaper or faster, who profited, and which regions it connected.

records.title: Market Revolution: Industrialization
records.heading: The market revolution
records.text:
The market revolution
Entrepreneurs organized production for distant markets, and factories began to replace work done at home.
Entrepreneurs helped to create a market revolution in production and commerce, in which market relationships between producers and consumers came to prevail as the manufacture of goods became more organized. Early in the century, most families still grew much of their own food and made many of their own goods. As the manufacture of goods became more organized, more people produced goods to sell to distant buyers and bought what they needed from others.
In New England, Samuel Slater opened a water-powered textile mill in Rhode Island in 1790. In the 1810s and 1820s the Boston Manufacturing Company in Waltham and the mills of Lowell, Massachusetts, brought spinning and weaving together under one roof. Investors formed corporations to raise money from many people. In many industries, the older putting-out system, in which merchants gave raw materials to families to work at home, gave way to factories.

records.title: Market Revolution: Industrialization
records.heading: Innovations in production
records.text:
Innovations in production
Machines and inventions raised the efficiency of manufacturing and farming and encouraged production for the market.
Innovations including textile machinery, steam engines, interchangeable parts, the telegraph, and agricultural inventions increased the efficiency of production methods. The power loom let mills weave cloth faster and more cheaply than home weavers. Steam engines powered boats and railroads and, in time, factories. Interchangeable parts, which Eli Whitney and other arms makers promoted, made goods easier to produce in quantity and to repair. Samuel Morse demonstrated the telegraph in 1844, and it let information travel almost instantly over long distances.
Agricultural inventions changed farming. Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) made it far easier to separate cotton fiber from its seeds. Cyrus McCormick's mechanical reaper (1834) let farmers harvest much more grain, and John Deere's steel plow (1837) cut through the heavy soil of the prairies. Such tools helped farmers raise crops for sale rather than for the family alone.

records.title: Market Revolution: Industrialization
records.heading: Transportation, government, and regional ties
records.text:
Transportation, government, and regional ties
Government-supported roads, canals, and railroads enlarged markets, linked the North and Midwest, and tied the South to Northern and British buyers and bankers.
Legislation and judicial systems supported the development of roads, canals, and railroads, which extended and enlarged markets and helped foster regional interdependence. States chartered companies and paid for canals, and the federal government helped to build the National Road. In Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) the Supreme Court held that Congress had the power to regulate interstate commerce, which ended a New York monopoly on steamboat travel. The Erie Canal (1825) joined the Hudson River with Lake Erie, lowered the cost of shipping goods between the Midwest and New York City, and helped to make New York the nation's leading port. Robert Fulton's steamboat, the Clermont (1807), proved that boats could travel upstream, and railroads such as the Baltimore and Ohio began running in 1830.
Transportation networks linked the North and Midwest more closely than they linked regions in the South. Midwestern farmers sent grain and livestock east and bought Northern manufactured goods. The South depended mostly on rivers that carried its cotton to ports. Increasing Southern cotton production and the related growth of Northern manufacturing, banking, and shipping industries promoted the development of national and international commercial ties. Southern cotton supplied New England and British mills, and Northern bankers, insurers, and shippers financed and carried the trade.
The market revolution did not affect every region in the same way. It tied the North and Midwest together by canals and railroads, while the South's economy rested on exporting cotton that was grown by enslaved labor.

records.title: Market Revolution: Society and Culture
records.text:
Market Revolution: Society and Culture
How the market revolution moved people to cities and to the West, divided Americans into new economic classes, and changed the roles of women and families.
The market revolution raised living standards for some Americans and left many others poor, and it reshaped where people lived, how they worked, and how families divided their roles.
The CED asks you to explain how innovation in technology, agriculture, and commerce affected different segments of American society. Always ask who gained, who lost, and who stayed outside the benefits.

records.title: Market Revolution: Society and Culture
records.heading: Migration and new communities
records.text:
Migration and new communities
Immigrants filled Northern cities and factories, and settlers built river towns in the West.
Large numbers of international migrants moved to industrializing Northern cities, while many Americans moved west of the Appalachians, developing thriving new communities along the Ohio and Mississippi rivers. Irish and German immigrants arrived in large numbers in the 1830s and 1840s. The Irish potato famine, which began in 1845, sent many Irish families to cities such as Boston and New York, where they took low-paying jobs in factories and construction and as domestic servants. Many Germans settled in Midwestern cities and farmland.
Many native-born Protestants reacted with nativism, a hostility toward immigrants, especially Catholics, which led to riots and the formation of anti-immigrant organizations. Meanwhile, Americans who crossed the Appalachians built towns and cities along the rivers. Cincinnati, Louisville, and St. Louis grew rapidly because river trade carried their goods to markets.

records.title: Market Revolution: Society and Culture
records.heading: Work, wealth, and class
records.text:
Work, wealth, and class
Factory work brought cash wages and prosperity for some, while a growing group of workers remained poor.
Increasing numbers of Americans, especially women and men working in factories, no longer relied on semi-subsistence agriculture. Instead they supported themselves by producing goods for distant markets. In Lowell and other mill towns, owners recruited young unmarried farm women, who lived in company boardinghouses and earned cash wages. When owners cut wages, some of these women held strikes in the 1830s, and by the 1840s many mills turned to immigrant workers.
The growth of manufacturing drove a significant increase in prosperity and standards of living for some. This led to the emergence of a larger middle class of merchants, professionals, clerks, and shopkeepers, and of a small but wealthy business elite, but also to a large and growing population of laboring poor. Many wage earners worked long hours in crowded conditions, and they formed unions to demand better pay and shorter hours. In Commonwealth v. Hunt (1842), the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court ruled that workers had the right to organize a union and to strike.

records.title: Market Revolution: Society and Culture
records.heading: Gender and family roles
records.text:
Gender and family roles
The market economy encouraged an ideal that separated men's public work from women's roles in the home, though many women did not live by it.
Gender and family roles changed in response to the market revolution, particularly with the growth of definitions of domestic ideals that emphasized the separation of public and private spheres. As work moved out of the home, many middle-class Americans came to see men as breadwinners in the public world of work and politics and women as the moral guardians of the home. Historians call this ideal the cult of domesticity or the cult of true womanhood. Magazines such as Godey's Lady's Book spread it, and the birthrate among middle-class families fell as families came to emphasize the care of fewer children.
This ideal gave women new influence in the home and in the education of children, and it encouraged new schools for girls, such as Emma Willard's Troy Female Seminary (1821). It also did not describe the lives of most women. Farm women, factory workers, immigrant domestic servants, and enslaved women all worked outside the ideal.
The separation of public and private spheres was an ideal that grew up mostly among middle-class families. It did not describe how all women lived or worked.

Expanding Democracy

records.title: Expanding Democracy
records.heading: Ending property requirements
records.text:
Ending property requirements
Property requirements fell as western states, wage earners, and competing parties pressed for the vote.
The nation's transition to a more participatory democracy was achieved by expanding suffrage from a system based on property ownership to one based on voting by all adult white men. At the nation's founding, most states required voters to own property or pay taxes. New western states, such as Indiana, Illinois, and Missouri, entered the Union with few or no property requirements. Older states revised their constitutions, and by the 1840s most states had dropped property requirements for white men.
Several developments explained the change. Many wage earners owned no land, and they argued that men who paid taxes and served in the militia should have a voice in government. Competing parties sought new voters, and the idea that the common man should have political influence became part of political life. In Rhode Island, which still used its colonial charter and limited the vote to landowners, Thomas Dorr led a movement in 1841–1842 that pressed for broader suffrage, and the state adopted a new constitution in 1843.

records.title: Expanding Democracy
records.heading: Party politics and participation
records.text:
Party politics and participation
Conventions, popular votes for electors, and mass campaigns made politics a mass activity.
The expansion of voting was accompanied by the growth of political parties. Parties nominated candidates at national conventions instead of in congressional caucuses, and the Anti-Masonic Party held the first national nominating convention in 1831. By 1832 every state but South Carolina chose presidential electors by popular vote. Parties organized parades, rallies, and newspapers, and they rewarded loyal supporters with government jobs, which became known as the spoils system.
The election of 1824 helped to bring about these changes. Andrew Jackson won the most popular and electoral votes but not a majority of electoral votes, and the House of Representatives chose John Quincy Adams. When Adams named Henry Clay secretary of state, Jackson's supporters charged that a “corrupt bargain” had denied the will of the voters. Jackson won in 1828, and voter turnout rose from about a quarter of eligible voters in 1824 to more than half in 1828 and to about 80 percent in 1840.

records.title: Expanding Democracy
records.heading: The limits of democracy
records.text:
The limits of democracy
Voting rights grew for white men, but women, free Black men, and American Indians were largely shut out.
The expansion of democracy was limited by race and sex. Many states took the vote away from free African American men even as they gave it to all white men. New York required free Black men, but not white men, to own property in 1821, and Pennsylvania excluded Black men entirely in 1838. Only a few New England states allowed Black men to vote on equal terms. In 1807 New Jersey ended the voting rights that some propertied women had held. Women could not vote anywhere, and American Indians were not citizens.
Do not describe the period as universal democracy. Suffrage became broader for white men and narrower for many free Black men.

records.text:
Jackson and Federal Power
How Andrew Jackson's presidency divided Democrats and Whigs over the national bank, tariffs, and federal power, and how Indian removal shaped relations with American Indian nations.
Under Jackson, a mass electorate debated the powers of the federal government, and the federal government used its power to remove American Indian nations from the Southeast.
The CED asks you to explain the causes and effects of continuing policy debates about the role of the federal government. Pair each debate with the party and region that took each side.

records.title: Jackson and Federal Power
records.heading: Democrats, Whigs, and the Bank War
records.text:
Democrats, Whigs, and the Bank War
Democrats and Whigs differed over the bank, tariffs, and internal improvements, and the Bank War made the divide sharper.
By the 1820s and 1830s, new political parties arose, the Democrats, led by Andrew Jackson, and the Whigs, led by Henry Clay, that disagreed about the role and powers of the federal government and issues such as the national bank, tariffs, and federally funded internal improvements. Democrats generally favored limited federal power, a more limited role for the national government in the economy, and the interests of farmers and workers. Whigs, who formed in opposition to what they called “King Andrew,” supported the American System of a national bank, a protective tariff, and federal funding of roads and canals.
Jackson's fight against the Second Bank of the United States showed the difference. Jackson saw the Bank as a monopoly that favored the wealthy. In 1832 he vetoed the bill to renew its charter, and he won reelection that year. He then removed federal deposits from the Bank and placed them in state banks, which critics called “pet banks.” A financial panic began in 1837, and it led to a depression that hurt the Democrats in the election of 1840.

records.title: Jackson and Federal Power
records.heading: The nullification crisis
records.text:
The nullification crisis
South Carolina's nullification challenge to the tariffs ended in a compromise but left the question of state authority unsettled.
Regional interests also shaped the federal power debate. Southerners disliked the protective tariffs of 1828 and 1832, which they thought raised the price of manufactured goods and favored the North. John C. Calhoun of South Carolina argued that a state could nullify, or declare void, a federal law that it judged unconstitutional. In November 1832 a South Carolina convention declared the tariffs null and void within the state.
Jackson rejected nullification as a threat to the Union and asked Congress to authorize force if needed. Congress passed the Force Act, and it also passed a compromise tariff in 1833 that lowered duties gradually. South Carolina then withdrew its nullification, though it also declared the Force Act null. The crisis ended without violence, but the question of whether states could resist federal law remained.

records.title: Jackson and Federal Power
records.heading: American Indian removal
records.text:
American Indian removal
The federal government forced Native nations out of the Southeast through laws, treaties, and force.
Frontier settlers tended to champion expansion efforts, while American Indian resistance led to a sequence of wars and federal efforts to control and relocate American Indian populations. Settlers in Georgia, Alabama, and Mississippi wanted the land of the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole, even though several of these nations had adopted written constitutions, farming, and some American customs. Jackson, who had fought the Creek in 1814 and the Seminole in 1818, supported removal.
Congress passed the Indian Removal Act in 1830, which gave the president the power to exchange land west of the Mississippi River for Native land in the East. The Supreme Court ruled in Worcester v. Georgia (1832) that Georgia could not extend its laws over the Cherokee Nation, but the federal government did not enforce the decision. In 1835 a small group of Cherokee signed the Treaty of New Echota, which most of the nation rejected, and in 1838–1839 the army forced about 16,000 Cherokee westward on the Trail of Tears, on which thousands died. Other nations resisted, as in the Black Hawk War (1832) and the Second Seminole War (1835–1842).
Removal was not carried out by settlers alone. The Indian Removal Act, treaties, and the army made it federal policy.

records.title: The Development of an American Culture
records.text:
The Development of an American Culture
How a national culture emerged between 1800 and 1848 from American subjects, European influences, and regional traditions, and how Romantic ideas shaped literature, art, philosophy, and architecture.
Americans created a national culture that blended American themes, European influences, and regional traditions, and many of its writers and artists believed in human perfectibility and in nature.
The CED asks you to explain how and why a new national culture developed. Place each writer, artist, or idea in its context: the new nation's search for its own identity, European Romanticism, and the market revolution.

records.title: The Development of an American Culture
records.heading: Blending American, European, and regional cultures
records.text:
Blending American, European, and regional cultures
National culture drew on American subjects, European models, and the traditions of regions.
A new national culture emerged that combined American elements, European influences, and regional cultural sensibilities. After the War of 1812, Americans felt a stronger desire for their own national identity. Noah Webster's dictionary (1828) and his earlier spelling books promoted an American form of English. Artists and writers chose American landscapes, history, and people as subjects, although they still borrowed styles and ideas from Europe.
Regional cultures also shaped the national culture. New England produced many writers and reformers, the South developed its own traditions and humor, and the frontier supplied folk heroes, songs, and stories.

records.title: The Development of an American Culture
records.heading: Romanticism in literature, art, and architecture
records.text:
Romanticism in literature, art, and architecture
Romantic ideas inspired American writers, painters, and architects who found national themes in nature and history.
Liberal social ideas from abroad and Romantic beliefs in human perfectibility influenced literature, art, philosophy, and architecture. Romanticism, a European movement, valued emotion, imagination, individualism, and nature over the rationalism of the Enlightenment. American writers such as Washington Irving, James Fenimore Cooper, Edgar Allan Poe, and Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote stories that drew on American settings and on imagination and moral questions.
Painters of the Hudson River School, including Thomas Cole, painted the grandeur of the American landscape, and many viewed the nation's wilderness as a source of national pride. In architecture, the Greek Revival style used columns and pediments to link the young republic to ancient Athens and Rome, which Americans saw as models of democracy and republican virtue.

records.heading: Transcendentalism and human perfectibility
records.text:
Transcendentalism and human perfectibility
Transcendentalists stressed individualism, intuition, and nature, and their belief in perfectibility supported reform.
Transcendentalism was an American philosophical and literary movement that grew out of Romanticism. Ralph Waldo Emerson, Henry David Thoreau, and Margaret Fuller argued that individuals could find truth through intuition and through nature, and that society should not demand conformity. Emerson's essay “Self-Reliance” (1841) urged people to trust themselves. These ideas reflected the Romantic belief in human perfectibility, and they encouraged many reformers who tried to improve individuals and society.
The new national culture was not wholly American in origin. Many of its leading ideas and styles, such as Romanticism, came from Europe and were adapted to American conditions.

records.title: The Second Great Awakening
records.text:
The Second Great Awakening
Why a wave of Protestant revivals swept the United States after 1800, and how the Second Great Awakening reshaped religion and set the stage for reform.
Democratic and individualistic beliefs, a response to rationalism, and the changes of the market revolution helped to produce a Protestant revival that emphasized individual choice and moral improvement.
The CED asks you to explain the causes of the Second Great Awakening. Separate the causes from the effects: causes lie in ideas and society before the revivals, and effects appear in reform and new churches.

records.title: The Second Great Awakening
records.heading: Causes of the Second Great Awakening
records.text:
Causes of the Second Great Awakening
Democratic ideas, a reaction against rationalism, and the disruption of the market revolution drew many Americans to revivals.
The rise of democratic and individualistic beliefs, a response to rationalism, and changes to society caused by the market revolution, along with greater social and geographical mobility, contributed to a Second Great Awakening among Protestants. Many Americans of the early republic believed that ordinary people could govern themselves, and they came to believe that ordinary people could also make their own religious choices.
Some Americans reacted against rationalism, the Enlightenment emphasis on reason, which had led some leaders to embrace Deism and Unitarianism. Others felt anxious about a rapidly changing society. As people moved to cities and to the West, away from the churches of their communities, revivals offered a sense of belonging and moral order.
