records.title: The Second Great Awakening
records.heading: Revivals and new religious movements
records.text:
Revivals and new religious movements
Camp meetings and preachers such as Finney spread revival, and new churches, including Black churches and the Latter-day Saints, grew from it.
Revivals spread through camp meetings, such as the large gathering at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, in 1801, and through preachers such as Charles Grandison Finney, who held revivals in western New York and in Northern cities in the 1820s and 1830s. Finney taught that individuals could choose salvation and could work to improve themselves and society. This view differed from the Calvinist belief in predestination. Methodist and Baptist churches grew rapidly because they accepted ordinary preachers and welcomed participation from many people.
The Awakening also produced new religious groups. Joseph Smith founded the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in 1830, and after its members faced hostility in several states, they migrated west. African Americans founded their own churches, such as the African Methodist Episcopal Church (1816), because they were often kept at the margins of white congregations. Women played a central role in the revivals, in church membership, and in religious organizations.

records.title: The Second Great Awakening
records.heading: Effects on American society
records.text:
Effects on American society
The Awakening encouraged individual improvement and inspired many reform efforts and new religious communities.
The Awakening influenced moral and social reforms and inspired utopian and other religious movements. Revivalists urged believers to improve themselves and to reform their society. Many converts joined movements for temperance, education, the abolition of slavery, and women's rights, which are the subject of Topic 4.11. The revivals reached the frontier and the settled East alike, and in the South many white and Black Southerners joined Methodist and Baptist congregations.
The Second Great Awakening was a cause of reform movements, not the same thing as reform. Keep the revivals separate from the movements they helped to inspire.

records.title: An Age of Reform
records.text:
An Age of Reform
How religious revival, voluntary organizations, abolitionism, and the women's rights movement tried to improve American society between 1800 and 1848.
Inspired by the Second Great Awakening and by democratic ideals, Americans formed voluntary organizations outside of government to improve society, and those efforts included antislavery and women's rights movements.
The CED asks you to explain how and why various reform movements developed and expanded. For each movement, name the problem it identified, who led it, how it worked outside government, and how much it achieved.

records.title: An Age of Reform
records.heading: Voluntary organizations and reform
records.text:
Voluntary organizations and reform
Voluntary groups worked outside government to reduce drinking, expand schools, reform asylums and prisons, and build model communities.
Americans formed new voluntary organizations that aimed to change individual behaviors and improve society through temperance and other reform efforts. The American Temperance Society (1826) urged Americans to give up alcohol, which reformers blamed for poverty, violence, and family suffering. Horace Mann in Massachusetts promoted public schools, and Dorothea Dix pressed states to build asylums to care for the mentally ill and to improve prisons.
The Second Great Awakening also inspired utopian communities, which tried to create model societies. Some, such as the Shakers, were religious, and others, such as New Harmony in Indiana and Brook Farm in Massachusetts, were based on cooperative ideals.

records.title: An Age of Reform
records.heading: Abolitionism and antislavery movements
records.text:
Abolitionism and antislavery movements
Abolitionists moved from gradual emancipation toward demands for immediate freedom, in the face of strong opposition.
Abolitionist and antislavery movements gradually achieved emancipation in the North, contributing to the growth of the free African American population, even as many state governments restricted African Americans' rights. By the 1820s most Northern states had abolished slavery or put it on the path to ending. Early antislavery efforts included the American Colonization Society (1816), which proposed sending free Black Americans to Africa, and most African Americans rejected this plan.
In the 1830s a more radical abolitionist movement called for immediate emancipation. William Lloyd Garrison began publishing The Liberator in 1831, and the American Anti-Slavery Society formed in 1833. Frederick Douglass, a formerly enslaved man, became one of the movement's greatest speakers. Antislavery movements increased in the North, but they faced hostility. Mobs attacked abolitionists, Congress adopted a rule in 1836 to table antislavery petitions without discussion, and many Northerners opposed equal rights for African Americans.

records.title: An Age of Reform
records.heading: The women's rights movement
records.text:
The women's rights movement
At Seneca Falls, reformers adapted the language of the Declaration of Independence to demand equal rights for women.
A women's rights movement sought to create greater equality and opportunities for women, expressing its ideals at the Seneca Falls Convention. Many of its leaders began in the temperance and antislavery movements, where women learned to organize but often found themselves restricted. In 1848 Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott organized the convention at Seneca Falls, New York. It adopted the Declaration of Sentiments, which was modeled on the Declaration of Independence and listed the ways in which women were denied rights, including the right to vote, to own property, and to receive an equal education.
Over time, arguments emerged over whether to narrow the goals to white women. Black women such as Sojourner Truth took part in the movement, but disagreements about race divided the movement in later decades.
Seneca Falls did not win the vote for women. It was the beginning of a long campaign that continued until the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.

records.title: African Americans in the Early Republic
records.text:
African Americans in the Early Republic
How enslaved people resisted and created communities, how free African Americans built institutions and joined antislavery efforts, and what stayed the same and changed in African American life from 1800 to 1848.
Enslaved and free African Americans built families, churches, and organizations, and they resisted slavery and discrimination, even as slavery expanded and legal restrictions on free Black Americans increased.
The CED asks you to explain the continuities and changes in the experience of African Americans. Ask what stayed constant, such as the force of slavery, and what changed, such as the growth of free Black institutions and abolitionist activity.

records.title: African Americans in the Early Republic
records.heading: Slavery and resistance
records.text:
Slavery and resistance
Rebellions failed and brought harsher laws, but enslaved people kept resisting in daily acts, while the internal slave trade split families.
Antislavery efforts in the South were largely limited to unsuccessful rebellions by enslaved people. Gabriel's plot in Virginia (1800) and Denmark Vesey's plot in Charleston (1822) were discovered and crushed. In 1831 Nat Turner led a rebellion in Southampton County, Virginia, in which about 55 white people were killed. The rebellion was put down, and many Black people were killed in revenge. Southern legislatures then tightened the slave codes and restricted the education and movement of enslaved and free Black people.
Enslaved people also resisted in everyday ways, by working slowly, breaking tools, pretending to be ill, or running away. Slavery grew and became more profitable as cotton spread. The Constitution allowed Congress to end the Atlantic slave trade in 1808, but the internal slave trade sold many enslaved people from the Upper South to the Deep South and broke up families.

records.title: African Americans in the Early Republic
records.heading: Families, religion, and community under slavery
records.text:
Families, religion, and community under slavery
Families, kin networks, religion, and secret learning helped enslaved people keep their dignity under slavery.
Enslaved blacks and free African Americans created communities and strategies to protect their dignity and family structures. Enslaved people formed families even though the law gave those families no protection and slaveholders could sell a husband, wife, or child. They kept kin ties across plantations, passed on names and stories, and helped relatives who had been sold away.
Religion was central. Enslaved people practiced Christianity in their own way, often in secret meetings, and they combined African traditions with Protestant faith in spirituals and sermons that emphasized hope and deliverance. Education was risky because Southern laws increasingly forbade teaching enslaved people to read, yet many learned secretly. Frederick Douglass later wrote of how he learned to read and why literacy became, for him, a pathway to freedom.

records.title: African Americans in the Early Republic
records.heading: Free Black communities and political activism
records.text:
Free Black communities and political activism
Free Black communities built institutions and joined antislavery efforts while facing discrimination in every region.
Free African Americans, who numbered more than 300,000 by 1830, lived in both North and South. They joined political efforts aimed at changing their status. In the North they built churches, such as Richard Allen's African Methodist Episcopal Church (1816), as well as schools, newspapers, and mutual aid societies. Black leaders held national conventions beginning in 1830, and David Walker's Appeal (1829) called on enslaved people to resist. Black abolitionists such as Frederick Douglass spoke and wrote against slavery. Free Black people and white allies also aided fugitives in the network known as the Underground Railroad.
Free African Americans faced severe restrictions. Northern states and towns segregated schools, churches, and transport, and some states took away their votes. Southern states limited their movement, and the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 put free Black people at risk of being seized. This was a period of both change, in the growth of free Black institutions and abolitionist activity, and continuity, in the power of slavery and racial prejudice.
Free Black Americans were not free from discrimination. They organized, but they also faced legal and social limits in both the North and the South.

records.title: The Society of the South in the Early Republic
records.text:
The Society of the South in the Early Republic
How cotton, soil exhaustion, and the westward movement of slavery shaped the South's economy, society, and sense of regional identity from 1800 to 1848.
The South tied its economy to cotton and slavery, expanded slavery into new lands as old fields wore out, and developed a regional identity that its leaders defended.
The CED asks you to explain how geographic and environmental factors shaped the development of the South. Link soil, climate, and rivers to crops, labor, migration, and the South's political and cultural defense of slavery.
records.excerpt: How cotton, soil exhaustion, and the westward movement of slavery shaped the South's economy, society, and sense of regional identity from 1800 to 1848.

records.title: The Society of the South in the Early Republic
records.heading: Cotton and Southern identity
records.text:
Cotton and Southern identity
Dependence on cotton and slave labor set the South apart from the North and shaped its regional identity.
Southern business leaders continued to rely on the production and export of traditional agricultural staples, contributing to the growth of a distinctive Southern regional identity. Cotton became the leading crop after the invention of the cotton gin in 1793 and the demand of British and New England textile mills. By the 1830s and 1840s cotton made up roughly half of the nation's exports by value, and the South's long growing season and warm, wet climate suited it well.
While the North built factories, canals, and railroads, the South invested its wealth in land and in enslaved laborers. It had fewer cities, banks, and factories, and fewer immigrants, than the North. Its economy relied on exports and on Northern and British merchants and bankers, and these differences encouraged white Southerners to see their region as distinct.

records.title: The Society of the South in the Early Republic
records.heading: Overcultivation and the westward movement of slavery
records.text:
Overcultivation and the westward movement of slavery
Soil exhaustion pushed planters west, and enslaved people were moved by force to new cotton lands.
As overcultivation depleted arable land in the Southeast, slaveholders began relocating their plantations to more fertile lands west of the Appalachians, where the institution of slavery continued to grow. Tobacco and cotton had worn out the soil of Virginia, the Carolinas, and Georgia. Planters moved to Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and later Texas, where the black soil of the Mississippi Valley and the Gulf plains was rich.
The movement was also a forced migration of enslaved people. Between 1790 and 1860 about a million enslaved people were moved from the Upper South to the Deep South, many by traders who sold them in markets such as Richmond and New Orleans, which broke up families. This westward expansion of slavery caused the contests over new territories discussed in Topic 4.3.

records.title: The Society of the South in the Early Republic
records.heading: Slavery as a Southern way of life
records.text:
Slavery as a Southern way of life
Planters led the South, and as abolitionism grew, Southern leaders defended slavery as a positive good and as part of their way of life.
In the South, although the majority of Southerners owned no enslaved persons, most leaders argued that slavery was part of the Southern way of life. About three-fourths of white Southern families owned no enslaved people, and many were yeoman farmers who grew food and some cotton on small farms. A small group of large planters held most of the enslaved people, most of the wealth, and most of the political power.
After the 1830s, as abolitionism grew in the North, many Southern leaders stopped calling slavery a necessary evil and began to defend it as a “positive good.” John C. Calhoun and others argued that slavery benefited both enslaved and enslavers. Proslavery writers used economics, religion, and claims about race to support their case. White Southerners who did not own slaves often supported slavery because they hoped to own slaves someday and because it gave them a claim to higher status than Black people.
Do not assume that most white Southerners owned enslaved people. Most owned none, but the large planters who did dominated Southern politics and economic life.

records.title: Causation in Period 4
records.text:
Causation in Period 4
A guide to explaining the causes and effects of change from 1800 to 1848, and to judging the extent to which politics, economics, and foreign policy promoted an American identity.
Politics, economics, and foreign policy all promoted a stronger sense of national identity from 1800 to 1848, but the same forces widened differences among regions, especially over slavery.
The CED treats causation as a historical reasoning process. The strongest answers identify a cause and an effect, explain how one led to the other, and judge the extent of the effect, using specific evidence.
records.excerpt: A guide to explaining the causes and effects of change from 1800 to 1848, and to judging the extent to which politics, economics, and foreign policy promoted an American identity.

records.title: Causation in Period 4
records.heading: How to reason about causation
records.text:
How to reason about causation
Name the cause, name the effect, explain the link, and judge how large the effect was.
Causation means explaining why something happened and what resulted. Begin by naming the event or development. Then name a cause, which is something that helped to bring it about, and an effect, which is something that followed from it. Strong answers separate long-term causes, such as the growth of a market economy, from short-term causes, such as a specific election or law.
A good causal claim explains the link between cause and effect and does not simply put them side by side. Avoid saying that one thing caused something else only because it came before it. Ask also how large the effect was. Questions about “the extent” of an effect call for you to say how much a factor mattered and what else mattered more.

records.title: Causation in Period 4
records.heading: Politics and foreign policy as causes of identity
records.text:
Politics and foreign policy as causes of identity
Participation, national courts, war, and expansion strengthened national identity, but regional interests and slavery pulled the country apart.
Politics promoted a shared identity when more citizens voted and took part in national campaigns. The expansion of suffrage and the rise of the Democrats and the Whigs gave many white men a sense of belonging to a nation. Supreme Court decisions such as McCulloch v. Maryland and Gibbons v. Ogden strengthened national authority over the states.
Foreign policy had similar effects. The War of 1812 stirred national pride and ended the Federalist Party. The Monroe Doctrine claimed a role for the United States in the Western Hemisphere. Territorial expansion, from the Louisiana Purchase to the removal of American Indians, gave Americans a sense of a continental destiny.
These same forces also divided. Regional interests shaped debates over the tariff and the bank, the nullification crisis showed how states could challenge federal power, and each addition of territory renewed the dispute over slavery, as the Missouri Compromise showed.

records.title: Causation in Period 4
records.heading: Economic change as a cause of identity
records.text:
Economic change as a cause of identity
The market revolution linked regions into one economy and created regional differences, so its effect on identity was mixed.
The market revolution tied together the country's economy. Canals, steamboats, railroads, and the telegraph linked the North and Midwest, and the sale of Southern cotton to Northern and British buyers tied the South to the national and international market. Consumers across the country bought goods from distant producers.
Economic change also produced differences. The North developed factories, wage labor, and cities, while the South relied on cotton and slave labor. These differences shaped political positions on tariffs, internal improvements, and the extension of slavery. In an essay about the extent to which politics, economics, and foreign policy promoted American identity, a balanced answer would say that each promoted a common identity among many Americans and that each also deepened regional differences.
A single cause rarely explains a large change. Combine causes, and say which mattered most and why.
